**It depends mainly on whether the truck has a working automatic overload prevention device.** The exclusion covers the equipment and activity, not the driver personally.

**Excluded from Subpart CC, §1926.1400(c)(17)(ii),** if all of these apply:
- It's an articulating/knuckle-boom truck crane delivering material to a construction site.
- It's transferring building supply **sheet goods or packaged materials** from the truck crane onto a structure. Sheetrock is specifically listed.
- It uses a **fork/cradle at the end of the boom**.
- The truck crane has a **properly functioning automatic overload prevention device**.

Your description meets the first three, including setting bundles on a 2nd floor deck. **If the device is missing or not working properly, this exclusion doesn't apply.** The ground-delivery exclusion in (c)(17)(i) won't cover it either, because that is for transfers from the truck crane to the ground without arranging materials in a particular sequence for hoisting.

**The exclusion also doesn't apply, §1926.1400(c)(17)(iii), if:**
- **(A)** The crane holds, supports or stabilizes material to facilitate a construction activity, such as holding it in place while it's attached.
- **(B)** The load is a prefabricated component, such as trusses, wall, floor or roof panels, or precast members.
- **(C)** The load is a structural steel member, such as joists, beams, columns or steel decking (bundled or unbundled), or a component of a systems-engineered metal building.
- **(D)** The activity isn't specifically excluded under (c)(17)(i) or (ii).

**Check on site:** confirm that the truck has the overload device and that it works. A load chart or the driver keeping within capacity isn't the same as that device. To verify how it works on a particular truck, you'll need the manufacturer's information.

Being excluded from Subpart CC doesn't by itself mean that no other OSHA requirements apply to the delivery.

**In construction, a forklift rigged this way is not exempt.** §1926.1400(c)(8) excludes powered industrial trucks (forklifts) **except when configured to hoist and lower (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.** Your setup fits that exception, so Subpart CC applies while the forklift is configured that way. See also the general scope in §1926.1400(a).

Check these before lifting:
- **Equipment changes:** §1926.1434 restricts modifications or additions that affect capacity or safe operation. It requires manufacturer approval or, in the situations and under the conditions it specifies, other qualified approval.
- **Capacity:** You can't exceed rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)). Load charts and procedures must be readily available (§1926.1417(c)). A standard fork rating doesn't show what the truck can safely handle with a suspended, swinging load.
- **Operator certification:** §1926.1427 generally requires certification or licensing, plus employer evaluation. Equipment with a maximum manufacturer-rated capacity of **2,000 lb or less** is excepted from §1926.1427 certification, but §1926.1441 has its own requirements, including operator training.
- **Other requirements:** Depending on the equipment and job, these include inspections (§1926.1412), power line safety (§§1926.1407–1411), signals (§1926.1419) and keeping people clear of loads (§1926.1425). Reduced requirements under §1926.1441 may apply at 2,000 lb or less.

**General industry (non-construction):** Subpart CC is a construction standard. §1910.180 covers crawler, locomotive and truck cranes, and I wouldn't treat it as covering your forklift. §1910.184 may apply to the slings you use. Forklift rules in §1910.178 are outside the regulations I answer from, so don't read this as an exemption or approval for non-construction work.

I can't tell you whether your particular attachment is approved or what it can lift. Get that from the forklift and attachment manufacturers. Is this for construction work, and what is the rated capacity of the setup?

**No. Setting roof trusses on your walls isn't an excluded delivery, so Subpart CC applies.** The knuckle-boom delivery exclusion doesn't apply to **prefabricated components, and roof trusses are named specifically** (§1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)). Because of that, **even unloading the trusses to the ground** isn't excluded. Holding a truss in place while it's attached also defeats the exclusion (§1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)). The exception for placing material onto a structure covers only building supply sheet goods or packaged materials, using a fork/cradle, with a working automatic overload prevention device (§1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)).

**Check these before the pick (not a complete list):**
- **Operator:** must be trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated by their employer, unless an exception applies. A crane with a maximum rated capacity of 2,000 lb or less is exempt from certification, but other requirements still apply (§§1926.1427, 1926.1441). A driver's license or delivery experience alone doesn't meet this.
- **Ground:** it must be firm, drained and graded enough, with supporting materials as needed, to meet the manufacturer's specifications for support and level. The controlling entity has duties here, including sharing known underground hazards (§1926.1402).
- **Power lines:** before operating, identify the work zone and determine whether any part of the crane, load line or load could get within 20 ft of a line. If so, one of the rule's options and its precautions must be met (§1926.1408(a)). Lines over 350 kV have added distance rules (§1926.1409).
- **Inspection:** the crane needs its shift inspection by a competent person (§1926.1412(d)), and its other required inspections must be current (§1926.1412(e)–(f)).
- **Capacity:** it must not exceed rated capacity, and the load weight must be determined as the rule requires (§1926.1417(o)).
- **Signals:** a signal person is required if the point of operation isn't in the operator's full view, the view is obstructed in the direction of travel, or the operator or person handling the load decides one is needed because of site-specific safety concerns (§1926.1419(a)). Signal persons must be qualified (§1926.1428).
- **Fall zone:** keep people from under the load as far as possible. Only those hooking, unhooking or guiding the load, making the initial connection, or doing certain concrete or hopper work may be in the fall zone (§1926.1425(b)). When a load is landed, only those needed to receive it may be there (§1926.1425(e)).
- **Rigging:** when your crew is in the fall zone hooking, unhooking, guiding or making the initial connection, a **qualified rigger** must rig the load. It must also be rigged to prevent unintentional displacement, and hooks must have self-closing, latching throats or the equivalent (§1926.1425(c)).

Your crew's fall protection and truss bracing also need to be planned. I haven't covered truss bracing or the general construction fall protection rules, which fall outside the regulations I answer from. For crane-related fall protection, see §1926.1423.

**Bottom line:** don't treat this as a favor during drop-off. Arrange it with the lumber yard ahead of time as a crane lift, and confirm the operator's qualifications, the crane's capacity at the needed radius and the items above. If they can't, don't have him set the trusses.

**No. A mobile crane with a luffing jib and/or tower attachment isn't considered a tower crane.** The definition of "tower crane" in **§1926.1401** expressly excludes it. The supplemental tower crane requirements in **§1926.1435** therefore don't apply just because of this configuration.

For construction work, follow the Subpart CC requirements that apply to your all-terrain crane as a mobile crane, including:

- **Assembly and disassembly:** §§1926.1403–1926.1406, plus §§1926.1407–1926.1411 for power line safety where applicable
- **Inspections:** §§1926.1412–1926.1413 (the latter covers wire rope)
- **Safety devices and operational aids:** §§1926.1415–1926.1416, including those for jibs and luffing jibs
- **Operation:** §1926.1417, including compliance with the manufacturer's procedures applicable to the crane's operation, and access to the load charts and other required information

This list isn't exhaustive. For the setup and operating limits of this configuration, check the crane's manufacturer procedures and load charts. I can't supply those from the regulations.

**No, that work is excluded from Subpart CC under §1926.1400(c)(4), as long as the conditions below are met.**

**The exclusion covers digger derricks used for:**
- Augering holes for poles carrying electric or telecommunication lines
- Placing and removing those poles
- Handling associated materials to be installed on or removed from the poles
- Any other work subject to 29 CFR 1926 Subpart V (electric power transmission and distribution)

**Conditions for the exclusion:**
- **Work subject to Subpart V:** the digger derrick use must comply with all applicable Subpart V requirements.
- **Construction work for telecommunication service** (as defined in §1910.268(s)(40)): the use must comply with all applicable requirements of §1910.268.

**Excluded from Subpart CC doesn't mean unregulated.** The Subpart V or §1910.268 requirements above still apply. This answer doesn't cover what those standards require.

**Other uses:** A digger derrick doing construction hoisting outside this exclusion isn't exempt under (c)(4) just because of the type of machine. For example, setting equipment or materials unrelated to the poles, on work not subject to Subpart V, wouldn't qualify. Check that job against Subpart CC's scope in §1926.1400(a) and the other exclusions in §1926.1400(c).

The controlling entity is defined in **§1926.1401** as an employer that is a **prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager, or any other legal entity which has the overall responsibility for the construction of the project: its planning, quality and completion.**

The test is overall responsibility for the project, not the job title. It also doesn't depend on who owns or operates the crane.

Its main related duties include ground conditions under **§1926.1402(c)**. The controlling entity must:
- **Ground preparation:** ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the §1926.1402(b) requirements are provided (§1926.1402(c)(1)).
- **Hazard information:** inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. This applies to hazards identified in documents in its possession (site drawings, as-built drawings, soil analyses), whether on site or off site, and to hazards otherwise known to it (§1926.1402(c)(2)).

**If there is no controlling entity** for the project, the §1926.1402(c)(1) requirement must be met by the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange for the ground preparations needed (§1926.1402(d)).

Other provisions in Subpart CC also assign duties to the controlling entity, including coordination where crane working radii overlap (§1926.1424(a)(3)).

**It's erection.** The definition of "assembly/disassembly" in **§1926.1401** says that for tower cranes, "erecting and climbing" replaces "assembly," and "dismantling" replaces "disassembly." It also says that **whether the crane is erected to full height at once or climbed in stages, increasing its height is an erection process.**

"Climbing" covers both adding tower sections (top climbing) and raising the whole crane within the structure (inside climbing) (§1926.1401).

For your jump, this means:
- **Follow the tower crane erecting, climbing and dismantling rules in §1926.1435(b).** These work together with the Subpart CC assembly/disassembly provisions that §1435(b) applies to tower cranes.
- **Meet the climbing-specific requirements in §1926.1435(b).** These apply before and during the climb and include following the manufacturer's prohibitions and having a registered professional engineer verify that the host structure can take the loads imposed on it.
- **Check the inspection requirements in §1926.1435(f)** along with the general inspection rules it references.

The actual climbing sequence, balancing and configuration limits depend on your crane. I can't give you those from these regulations.

**Engine pull: Subpart CC doesn't apply. Rebar: it does.**

**Pulling the dozer engine:** §1926.1400(c)(9) excludes a mechanic's truck with a hoisting device **when used in activities related to equipment maintenance and repair**. Pulling an engine for repair fits. This only removes the lift from Subpart CC. It doesn't mean no other safety rules apply.

**Setting rebar bundles:** This isn't equipment maintenance or repair, so the exclusion doesn't cover it. A truck crane that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load falls under §1926.1400(a). The exclusion depends on the **activity**, not the truck.

What applies then depends on the crane's **rated hoisting/lifting capacity**:

- **2,000 lb or less:** §1926.1441 sets a reduced set of requirements in place of most of Subpart CC. It still covers matters such as power line safety, operation and safety devices, and operator training. It is **not** a full exemption. These cranes are excepted from the operator certification requirements.
- **Over 2,000 lb:** The applicable Subpart CC requirements apply, including:
  - **Operator:** trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated under §1926.1427, subject to that section's exceptions and provisions for operators-in-training
  - **Power lines:** assess the work zone before operating (§1926.1408(a))
  - **Inspections:** including each shift and the periodic inspections (§1926.1412)
  - **Capacity:** don't exceed rated capacity, and know the load's weight (§1926.1417(o))
  - **Ground conditions:** adequate to support the crane (§1926.1402)
  - **Signals:** a qualified signal person when required, such as when the operator's view is obstructed (§§1926.1419 and 1926.1428)
  - **People and loads:** swing radius and fall zone protections (§§1926.1424 and 1926.1425)
  - **Rigging:** a qualified rigger is specifically required in certain cases, including when workers are in the fall zone to hook, unhook, guide or initially connect a load (§1926.1425(c))

**Check before the rebar lift:** find the crane's rated capacity and confirm the operator meets the requirements for it. A light bundle doesn't put a higher-rated crane under the 2,000 lb provision. For capacity at a given radius and setup, use that crane's load chart, which I don't have.

This assumes the work is construction. General industry work falls under Part 1910 instead.

response.text:
**1. Magnet or man basket: yes, Subpart CC still applies** when the equipment is covered and used in construction. Under §1926.1400(b), covered equipment stays covered when used with attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended. The list includes **magnets** and **personnel platforms**, as well as hooks, grapples, buckets, augers or drills, and pile driving equipment. The list isn't exhaustive.

A man basket also brings in **§1926.1431 (hoisting personnel)**. Under §1926.1431(a), using covered equipment to hoist employees is **prohibited** unless the employer demonstrates that conventional means of reaching the work area (such as a ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform or scaffold) would be **more hazardous, or isn't possible** because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions. Other requirements in §1926.1431 also apply, and it has specific exceptions to this test, so check it before planning the lift.

**2. Chainfall: machinery that hoists using a chainfall is excluded** from Subpart CC under §1926.1400(c), as is machinery that hoists using a come-a-long. I believe this is paragraph (c)(10).

**There is a rule, and eyeballing alone doesn't show you meet it.** For construction, **§1926.1402(b)** says the equipment must not be **assembled or used** unless the ground is **firm, drained and graded** enough that, with supporting materials if necessary, the **manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level** are met. The drainage requirement doesn't apply to marshes or wetlands.

- **No universal number:** §1926.1402 doesn't set a bearing pressure or level tolerance. Get the support and level specs from your crane's manufacturer. I can't give them from these regulations.
- **What counts:** Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing and marsh buggies (in marshes/wetlands) or similar devices (§1926.1402(a)).
- **Ground prep:** The controlling entity must ensure the necessary preparations are provided (§1926.1402(c)(1)). If there's no controlling entity, this falls to the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange them (§1926.1402(d)).
- **Hidden hazards:** The controlling entity must tell the equipment user and operator where hazards are beneath the setup area, such as voids, tanks or utilities. This covers hazards identified in documents it has, on or off site (such as site drawings, as-builts or soil analyses), and hazards it otherwise knows about (§1926.1402(c)(2)).
- **Ground not good enough:** If the A/D (assembly/disassembly) director or operator determines it doesn't meet (b), that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity (§1926.1402(e)). Don't assemble or use the crane until (b) is met.

**Outriggers or stabilizers (§1926.1404(q))**
- They must be fully extended or, if the load chart permits, deployed as it specifies.
- They must be set to remove the equipment's weight from the wheels, except on locomotive cranes.
- Floats, if used, must be attached to the outriggers or stabilizers.
- Blocking under the floats must be strong enough to prevent crushing, bending or shear failure.
- It must also be thick, wide and long enough to completely support the float, transmit the load to the ground, and prevent shifting, toppling or excessive settlement under load.

This answer covers construction. If your job falls under general industry (Part 1910), don't assume §1926.1402 is the governing rule.

**Yes, you can use a company assembly/disassembly procedure, with conditions. Synthetic slings add rigging requirements, but they don't by themselves rule out your procedure.**

**Company procedure (§1926.1403)**
- You must comply with all applicable **manufacturer prohibitions**, whichever procedure you use.
- Otherwise, you may follow either the manufacturer's procedures or your own (§1926.1403(a)–(b)).
- You may use your own only if you can **demonstrate** that it meets §1926.1406.

**Your procedure must:**
- Prevent unintended dangerous movement and collapse of any part of the equipment (§1926.1406(a)(1))
- Provide adequate support and stability for all parts (§1926.1406(a)(2))
- Position employees involved in assembly/disassembly to minimize their exposure to unintended movement or collapse (§1926.1406(a)(3))
- Be developed by a **qualified person** (§1926.1406(b))

The other applicable assembly/disassembly requirements, including those in §1926.1404, still apply. For example, the work must be directed by an A/D supervisor who meets the criteria in §1926.1404(a).

**Synthetic slings used for assembly/disassembly rigging**
- A **qualified rigger** must do the rigging work (§1926.1404(r)(1)).
- Protect the slings from abrasive, sharp or acute edges, and from configurations that could reduce rated capacity, such as distortion or localized compression (§1926.1404(r)(2)).
- Follow the **synthetic sling manufacturer's** instructions, limitations, specifications and recommendations (§1926.1404(r)(3)). Your company procedure can't override them.
- Other applicable rigging rules, including §1926.251, also apply (§1926.1404(r)).

**Yes. In construction, if you're doing the assembly alone, you must meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person.** You're then considered the assembly/disassembly (A/D) director (§1926.1404(a)(2)).

**What those terms mean (§1926.1401):**
- **Competent person:** can identify existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions that are unsanitary, hazardous or dangerous to employees, **and** has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them.
- **Qualified person:** has a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, **or** has extensive knowledge, training and experience, and has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work or the project.

Experience or an operator certification doesn't by itself show that you meet both definitions.

**As A/D director:**
- **Procedures:** You must follow the manufacturer's procedures and prohibitions or, where permitted, employer procedures (§1926.1403). Employer procedures must meet §1926.1406.
- **Knowledge:** You must understand the applicable procedures (§1926.1404(b)).
- **Review:** You must review them immediately before starting, unless you understand them and have applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment, including accessories (§1926.1404(c)).
- **Other requirements:** The rest of §1926.1404 still applies where relevant. Check power line precautions before assembly (§1926.1407).

**Before the crane is used:** A qualified person must inspect it after assembly to confirm it's configured according to the manufacturer's equipment criteria. If those criteria are unavailable, §1926.1412(c) sets out how they must be developed.

This answer applies to construction work under Subpart CC. I can't give you the jib installation steps without the manufacturer's procedure.

**Yes, but only as a narrow exception.** The default rule is that when pins or similar devices are being removed, employees **must not be under the boom, jib or other components** (§1926.1404(f)(1)).

**Exception (§1926.1404(f)(2)):** This applies only where **the employer demonstrates that site constraints require** one or more employees to be under the boom, jib or components during pin removal. The **A/D (assembly/disassembly) director** must then implement procedures that:
- **minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement**, and
- **minimize both the duration and the extent** of exposure under the boom.

Non-mandatory **Appendix B** to Subpart CC gives an example. A tight site or convenience alone isn't enough: the constraints must actually *require* someone to be under there. If the pins can be driven from outside the boom, or the work can be set up so no one has to go under, I wouldn't treat the exception as met.

**Related requirements before anyone knocks a pin:**
- **A/D director:** Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons (§1926.1404(a)).
- **Procedures:** The employer must follow the manufacturer's procedures and prohibitions, or employer procedures where permitted (§1926.1403). Employer procedures must meet §1926.1406. The §1404(f)(2) exception doesn't waive these.
- **Crew briefing:** Before starting, crew members must understand their tasks, the associated hazards, and the hazardous positions or locations to avoid (§1926.1404(d)(1)).
- **Specific hazards:** The A/D director must address the applicable hazards in §1926.1404(h), including support and blocking adequacy, boom and jib pick points, center of gravity, and stability on pin removal.

These regulations can't tell you which pins are safe to remove, or what blocking or support this crawler needs. That depends on the manufacturer's procedure or compliant employer procedures and the actual configuration. **If you don't have that and an A/D director's procedure for working under the boom, don't go under it.**

**Test the boom hoist brake before anyone relies on it.** The test must show whether the brake is sufficient to prevent boom movement (§1926.1404(h)(10)).

**If it isn't sufficient,** you must use one of these to prevent dangerous boom movement from a brake failure (§1926.1404(h)(10)):
- A boom hoist pawl
- Another locking device or backup braking device
- Another method, such as blocking the boom or using an assist crane

**Also covered for the people working on it:**
- **Who addresses the hazard:** Assembly/disassembly (A/D) must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons (§1926.1404(a)(1)). - **Out of the operator's view:** This applies when a crew member goes out of the operator's view and is in, on or under the equipment, or near it or the load, where movement could injure them. The crew member must tell the operator before going there. An operator who knows someone went there must not move any part of the equipment until informed, through a pre-arranged communication system, that the crew member is in a safe position (§1926.1404(e)).
- **Under the boom:** If pins or similar devices are being removed, employees must not be under the boom, jib or other components unless site constraints require it. In that case, the A/D director must implement procedures that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom (§1926.1404(f)). A tested brake doesn't remove these requirements.

You must also follow either the manufacturer's A/D procedures or compliant employer procedures (§1926.1403). These regulations don't give the test steps for your particular crane, so I can't provide them from here. Check the procedures you're using and the manufacturer's information.

**There's no default OSHA length, number of sections or rule of thumb.** The cantilever rule in §1926.1404, "Cantilevered boom sections" (I believe it's paragraph (j), but check the letter against the current text), says:

- You must not exceed the **manufacturer's limit** on the amount of boom supported only by cantilevering.
- If that limit is unavailable, a **registered professional engineer (RPE) familiar with that type of equipment** must determine it **in writing**, and you must not exceed it.

**A missing manual doesn't prove the limit is unavailable.** First try the manufacturer, or its successor, with the make, model, serial number and boom configuration. If you can't get the limit, get the RPE's written determination before cantilevering any boom. A competent or qualified person's estimate, or past practice on this crane, doesn't meet this requirement.

**Other requirements for the job**
- **Assembly/disassembly procedures:** You can use the manufacturer's procedures or your own (§1926.1403). Your own must meet §1926.1406, including development by a qualified person. They don't replace the RPE determination for the cantilever limit.
- **Supervision:** An A/D director who meets the competent and qualified person criteria, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons, must direct the work (§1926.1404(a)).
- **Under the boom:** When pins are being removed, workers must not be under the boom, jib or other components, except where site constraints require it. In that case, the A/D director must implement procedures that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and the duration and extent of exposure (§1926.1404(f)).
- **Hazards to address:** These include blocking and its location, pick points, center of gravity and stability when pins are removed (§1926.1404(h)).

The missing manual may also affect operation. The load chart and other required operating information must be readily available in the cab, or at the control station if there's no cab (§1926.1417(c)). An RPE's cantilever limit doesn't satisfy that requirement.

**Yes, the assist crane loads must be verified before assembly begins.** The A/D (assembly/disassembly) supervisor must address both this and the blocking (§1926.1404(h)).

**Blocking**
- **Material:** The size, amount, condition and method of stacking must be sufficient to sustain the loads and maintain stability (§1926.1404(h)(2)).
- **Location:** Blocking that supports lattice booms or components must be placed to protect the equipment's structural integrity **and** to prevent dangerous movement and collapse (§1926.1404(h)(3)(i)–(ii)).
- **Ground:** Site and ground conditions must be adequate for safe assembly, including ground that can support the equipment. If they aren't, assembly must not begin (§1926.1404(h)(1)).

The paragraphs on blocking material and location are performance standards. They give no specific cribbing dimensions, stacking height or safety factor.

**Assist crane loads**
The loads imposed on the assist crane **at each phase** of assembly or disassembly must be verified under §1926.1417(o)(3) **before assembly or disassembly begins** (§1926.1404(h)(4)). Section 1926.1417(o)(3) requires verifying that the load is within rated capacity by at least one of these methods:
- **Determine the weight** from an industry-recognized source (such as the load's manufacturer), by an industry-recognized calculation method, or by other equally reliable means. The information must be given to the operator before the lift if the operator asks (§1926.1417(o)(3)(i)).
- **Begin hoisting and check** with a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator or rated capacity limiter whether the load exceeds 75% of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used. If it does, don't proceed until the weight is verified under (o)(3)(i) (§1926.1417(o)(3)(ii)).

Because (h)(4) requires verification before the work starts, I wouldn't plan on checking by trial hoist partway through assembly. Work out each phase's loads in advance. That is my practical reading, not separate wording in the rule.

- **Pick points:** Attachment points for slinging the boom and jib sections, and whether the sections can be lifted from them, must be addressed (§1926.1404(h)(5)).

**Who writes it:** a **qualified person** (§1926.1406(b)). Under §1926.1401, that means someone who, by a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, or by extensive knowledge, training and experience, has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve problems relating to the subject matter, the work or the project.

**What it must cover (§1926.1406(a)).** The procedures must:
1. Prevent unintended dangerous movement and collapse of any part of the equipment (a)(1).
2. Provide adequate support and stability for all parts of the equipment (a)(2).
3. Position employees involved in assembly/disassembly so their exposure to unintended movement or collapse of part or all of the equipment is minimized (a)(3).

**Conditions on using your own (§1926.1403):**
- You may use them only if you can **demonstrate** that they meet §1926.1406.
- You must still comply with **all applicable manufacturer prohibitions**.
- If you use synthetic slings for assembly/disassembly rigging, you must follow the manufacturer's synthetic sling instructions, limitations, specifications and recommendations (§1926.1403 note; §1926.1404(r)).

**Other requirements that still apply** include these from §1926.1404:
- **A/D director (a):** Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons.
- **Procedure review (b):** The director must understand the procedures. The director must also review them immediately before starting, unless they understand them and have applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment, including accessories.
- **Crew instructions (d):** Before starting, the director must ensure crew members understand their tasks, the associated hazards, and any hazardous positions or locations to avoid.
- **Specific hazards (h):** The director must address the listed hazards, such as site and ground bearing conditions, blocking, boom and jib pick points, center of gravity, stability on pin removal, snagging, struck-by from counterweights, boom hoist brake failure, backward stability, and wind and weather. Check (h) for the full list and its details.
- **Components and configuration (m):** Selections affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer instructions, prohibitions, limitations and specifications. If those are unavailable, an RPE familiar with the equipment type must approve the selection and configuration in writing. The other route is an approved modification meeting §1926.1434. Writing your own procedure doesn't remove this requirement.

This isn't all of §1926.1404. Also check **§1926.1405** if you're dismantling booms or jibs, and **§1926.1435** for tower cranes, which have additional provisions.

§1926.1406 doesn't itself state that the procedures must be in writing. Documenting them can help you show they comply, but that's practical advice rather than a stated requirement of that section.

**I can't give you a yes or no from these regulations.** I know of no provision in Subpart CC or §§1910.179, .180 or .184 that specifically says a jib must come off, or may stay on, during pile driving. That doesn't mean leaving it on is allowed.

These Subpart CC rules bear on the decision:

- **Manufacturer's procedures:** The employer must comply with all manufacturer procedures applicable to the equipment's operational functions, including its use with attachments (§1926.1417(a)). Check the operator's manual and any manufacturer instructions for pile driving and for the jib, whether erected or stowed.
- **If those procedures are unavailable:** The employer must develop and ensure compliance with the procedures needed for safe operation of the equipment and attachments (§1926.1417(b)(1)). Procedures for operational controls must be developed by a qualified person (§1926.1417(b)(2)). Procedures related to the equipment's capacity must be developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment (§1926.1417(b)(3)).
- **Capacity information:** Rated capacities and related operating information, instructions and warnings must be readily available in the cab (§1926.1417(c)). Check what they require for your jib configuration, including any capacity deductions.
- **Dedicated pile drivers:** Subpart CC applies to them, with the qualifications in §1926.1439. This doesn't settle the jib question.

**Before driving:** Confirm the manufacturer allows pile driving in your exact configuration. If you can't confirm it, raise that with the employer and resolve it under the rules above before work starts.

OSHA's separate pile driving rule, §1926.603, is outside the regulations I cover, as are consensus standards such as ASME B30.5. Have someone check those, along with your contract and site requirements, since any of them may address this.

**Lifting off the wheels:** No. Outriggers or stabilizers generally must be set to remove the equipment weight from the wheels, but **locomotive cranes are excepted** (§1926.1404(q)(2)). - **under the outrigger or stabilizer float/pad of the jack**, or

- **Blocking itself:** It must also meet the blocking requirements that (q)(5)(i) cross-references in §1926.1404(h).

The ground under the cribbing also matters. It must be firm, drained and graded enough that, with supporting materials if needed, the manufacturer's specifications for support and level are met (§1926.1402(b)).

**No. With the pendants in tension, neither set of pins may be removed, even partly.** This applies to dismantling to change boom length, so shortening the stick is covered.

**§1926.1405:**
- **(a):** No pendant pins may be removed, partly or completely, while the pendants are in tension.

**15 feet** is the minimum for a 138 kV line under Table A (over 50 to 200 kV), per §1926.1408, Table A. I'm taking "stick" to mean the boom. The 15 ft applies to **any part of the equipment, load line or load**, including rigging and lifting accessories. It's a limit you must not breach, so plan for extra room.

**Conditions during crane operations:**
- **Work zone:** First identify it and determine whether any part of the equipment, load line or load, at up to maximum working radius in the work zone, could get closer than **20 ft**. If so, you must use one of the options in §1926.1408(a)(2): deenergize and ground, keep 20 ft, or use Table A (§1926.1408(a)(1)-(2)).
- **Voltage:** To use Table A, determine the line's voltage (§1926.1408(a)(2)(iii)). The utility owner/operator must provide it within 2 working days of the employer's request (§1926.1408(c)).
- **Encroachment prevention:** If any part could get closer than 15 ft, the employer must take the measures in §1926.1408(b). These include:
  - a planning meeting
  - nonconductive tag lines, if tag lines are used
  - an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs, with the limited substitute the rule allows when the operator can't see it
- **Additional measure:** §1926.1408(b) also requires at least one of these: a proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, range control warning device, range limiting device or insulating link.

**Other situations:**
- **Assembly or disassembly:** See §1926.1407. No part may get closer than the clearance allowed under the option chosen there.
- **Traveling with no load:** §1926.1411 and Table T have different clearances.
- **Working closer than 15 ft:** This is allowed only if the employer meets all of §1926.1410, including showing that staying at Table A distance is infeasible.
- **Power transmission and distribution work:** Different provisions can apply, so check the scope of the job.

**No. Keeping the Table A distance doesn't allow assembly under the line.** No part of the crane, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories), whether partially or fully assembled, may be below a power line **unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized it and visibly grounded it at the worksite** (§1926.1407(c)). This covers boom sections being laid out and pinned on the ground. Table A is not an exception, however much vertical clearance you have.

**Your options**
- **Stay under the line:** First get confirmation that the utility has deenergized the line and visibly grounded it at the worksite. A line is presumed energized until then (§1926.1407(e), applying §1926.1408(e)).
- **Move the layout out from under the line:** Before assembly, determine whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than 20 feet to a line in the assembly area or direction. If it could, use one of these (§1926.1407(a)):
  - **Option 1:** Deenergize and ground.
  - **Option 2:** Keep 20 feet of clearance, using the encroachment-prevention measures in §1926.1407(b).
  - **Option 3:** Determine the line voltage and the Table A distance. If any part could get closer than that, use the §1926.1407(b) measures to keep it from doing so.

**Measures under §1926.1407(b)**
- Hold a planning meeting with the assembly/disassembly director, operator, crew and other workers in the area. Review the line location and the steps to prevent encroachment and electrocution.
- If you use tag lines, they must be nonconductive.
- Add at least one of these:
  - a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator
  - a proximity alarm
  - a range control warning device
  - a range limiting device
  - an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs

**Table A for energized lines at typical distribution voltages:** The minimum is **10 feet up to 50 kV** and **15 feet over 50 to 200 kV** (Table A, §1926.1408). Don't assume the voltage just because it's a "distribution line." Under Option 3, get it from the utility. No part may be closer than the Table A distance unless the utility has deenergized and visibly grounded the line (§1926.1407(d)).

The same below-line and Table A prohibitions apply during **disassembly**. When planning the layout, account for the boom's full path during assembly and raising, not just where the sections sit on the ground.

# Power lines during assembly and disassembly: §1926.1407

## What to determine before assembly (§1926.1407(a))
Could any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) get **closer than 20 feet** to a power line, in the direction or area of assembly, during assembly? The same check applies before disassembly. If so, you must use one of these three options.

## Your options

| Option | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **1: De-energize and ground** (§1926.1407(a)(1)) | Confirm from the utility owner/operator that the line has been de-energized and is visibly grounded at the worksite. |
| **2: 20-foot clearance** (§1926.1407(a)(2)) | Keep everything at least 20 ft away, using the measures in §1926.1407(b). |
| **3: Table A clearance** (§1926.1407(a)(3)) | Determine the line's voltage and the Table A distance, then determine whether anything could get closer than that. If so, use the §1926.1407(b) measures to prevent it. |

**Table A (§1926.1408)**

| Voltage (kV, AC) | Minimum clearance |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 | Set by the utility owner/operator, or a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person for electrical power transmission and distribution |

For Option 3, the utility owner/operator must provide the requested voltage information **within 2 working days** of your request (§1926.1407(e)).

## Encroachment measures for Options 2 and 3 (§1926.1407(b))
In Option 3, these apply if something could get closer than the Table A distance.

- **Planning meeting:** Include the assembly/disassembly (A/D) director, operator, assembly crew and other workers in the A/D area. Review the line locations and the steps to prevent encroachment and electrocution.
- **Tag lines:** If used, they must be nonconductive.
- **At least one of these:**
  1. **Dedicated spotter** in continuous contact with the operator. The spotter must:
     - have a visual aid for judging the clearance, such as a painted ground line, stanchions or line-of-sight landmarks
     - be positioned to gauge the distance effectively
     - where necessary, use equipment to communicate directly with the operator
     - give the operator timely information so the clearance is maintained
  2. **Proximity alarm** set to give enough warning to prevent encroachment.
  3. **Automatic warning device**, such as a range control warning device, that tells the operator when to stop, set to give enough warning to prevent encroachment.
  4. **Automatic range-limiting device** set to prevent encroachment.
  5. **Elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs** in the operator's view, with flags or similar high-visibility markings.

## Limits regardless of option
- **Below a line:** No part of the crane, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) may be below a power line during A/D unless you've confirmed the utility has de-energized it and visibly grounded it at the worksite (§1926.1407(c)).
- **Inside Table A:** Nothing may get closer than the Table A distance unless you've confirmed the same (§1926.1407(d)).
- **Presume energized:** Treat every line as energized unless the utility confirms it has been and continues to be de-energized, and it is visibly grounded at the worksite (§1926.1407(f)).
- **Warning postings:** Post at least one electrocution warning in the cab, in the operator's view. Except on overhead gantry and tower cranes, also post at least two on the outside of the equipment (§1926.1407(g)).

Once the crane is assembled, check the separate rules for operations near power lines (§1926.1408).

## Assembly/disassembly (§1926.1407)
These precautions apply when you use Option (2), 20-foot clearance, or when Option (3), Table A clearance, requires them because part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than the Table A distance (§1926.1407(a)). You need **all** of the following:
- **Planning meeting:** include the A/D director, operator, A/D crew and other workers in the A/D area, and review the line locations and how to prevent encroachment and electrocution (§1926.1407(b)(1)).
- **Tag lines:** if used, they must be nonconductive (§1926.1407(b)(2)).
- **At least one additional measure** (§1926.1407(b)(3)):
  - a dedicated spotter
  - a proximity alarm
  - a range control warning device
  - a range-limiting device
  - an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs

To count, the warning line must be **elevated, in view of the operator, and equipped with flags or similar high-visibility markings**. A painted ground line alone doesn't meet this description, although it can be a spotter's visual aid.

## Operations (§1926.1408)

**If this is the power line warning line, you need a dedicated spotter *plus* one more protective measure** (§1926.1408(b)(3)). The spotter alone isn't enough.

**1. Use a dedicated spotter** who is in continuous contact with the operator. The spotter must (§1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)):
- have a visual aid to identify the minimum clearance distance, such as a painted line on the ground, a line of stanchions or line-of-sight landmarks
- be positioned to effectively gauge the clearance
- where necessary, use equipment to communicate directly with the operator
- give timely information so the operator can maintain the required clearance

The spotter must also meet the signal person qualifications in §1926.1428, and their **sole responsibility** is watching the separation between the power line and the equipment, load line and load (§1926.1401, "Dedicated spotter").

**2. Also use at least one of these** (§1926.1408(b)(4)):
- (i) proximity alarm
- (iii) device that automatically warns the operator when to stop, such as a range control warning device
- (iv) device that automatically limits range of movement
- (v) insulating link/device between the end of the load line and the load

**The other precautions still apply** (§1926.1408(b)(1)–(3)):
- Hold a planning meeting with the operator and the other workers who will be in the area of the equipment or load, to review the line location and the steps to prevent encroachment and electrocution.
- Any tag lines must be non-conductive.
- Keep an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs, with flags or similar high-visibility markings. The spotter doesn't replace it. Place it **20 ft** from the line under Option (2), or at the **Table A distance** under Option (3) (§1926.1408(a)).

An insulating link/device installed between the end of the load line (or below) and the load is one of the listed measures, and you need at least one (§1926.1408(b)(4)(v)). This applies when you use Option (2), 20-foot clearance, or Option (3), Table A clearance, under §1926.1408(a)(2).

**A fixed-length lattice boom is a non-extensible boom, so the exception is in §1926.1408(d)(2)(ii).**

**General rule, §1926.1408(d)(1):** No part of the equipment, load line or load, including rigging and lifting accessories, is allowed below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized it and visibly grounded it at the worksite, or a (d)(2) exception applies.

**Non-extensible boom exception, §1926.1408(d)(2)(ii):** The employer must demonstrate that **the uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom at true vertical,** would be **more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line, or more than the Table A minimum clearance distance below that plane.**

**Table A clearances (voltage in kV, AC):**

| Voltage | Minimum clearance |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 | As established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution |

**Applying it:**
- Check the height **with the boom at true vertical**, even if you plan to work at a lower boom angle. Keeping the boom low, or using a procedure that limits boom angle, doesn't meet this exception.
- The result must be **more than** the required distance, so exactly that distance isn't enough.
- The rule text offers 20 ft "or" the Table A distance. Above 350 kV, Table A is greater than 20 ft, so confirm the voltage. As a conservative practice, I'd use at least the Table A distance for those lines.

**Other exceptions in §1926.1408(d)(2):**
- The work is covered by Subpart V (paragraph (d)(2)(i)).
- The employer demonstrates that complying with (d)(1) is infeasible and meets the requirements of §1926.1410 (paragraph (d)(2)(iv)).

Paragraph (d)(2)(iii) covers articulating or extensible booms.

**By default, no.** No part of the crane, load line or load, including rigging and lifting accessories, may be below a power line unless your employer has **confirmed that the utility owner/operator has de-energized it and visibly grounded it at the worksite** (§1926.1408(d)(1)).

**Exceptions (the employer has to show one applies, §1926.1408(d)(2)):**
1. **High enough line, (d)(2)(iii):** With the boom **fully extended and at true vertical**, the crane's uppermost part would still be **more than the minimum clearance distance below the plane of the line**. What you *plan* to extend doesn't count. A line that just looks way up there doesn't qualify either.
2. **Subpart V work, (d)(2)(i):** The work is covered by Subpart V (electric power transmission and distribution).
3. **Infeasible, (d)(2)(iv):** The employer shows that complying with (d)(1) is infeasible **and** meets all of §1926.1410. Being inconvenient isn't enough.

**Table A clearances (§1926.1408):**

| Line voltage (AC) | Minimum clearance |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 kV | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 kV | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 kV | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 kV | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 kV | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 kV | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 kV | Set by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in power transmission and distribution |

**Check for exception 1:** Line height minus the crane's maximum vertical reach must be **more than** the clearance. For example, with a line of 50 kV or less, a lowest point of 60 ft and a max tip height of 48 ft *from the ground as set up*, you have 12 ft, which is more than 10. A max tip height of 50 ft leaves exactly 10 ft, which doesn't qualify. These are made-up numbers. As practical cautions, use the line's lowest point near your work, allow for sag and movement, and don't measure with anything that could get near the line. Get your crane's maximum height from the manufacturer's data; I can't give it.

**Also:** Assume the line is energized unless the utility confirms it's de-energized and it's visibly grounded at the worksite (§1926.1408(e)). Passing exception 1 only lifts the ban on being below the line. Keep the crane, load line and load out of the required clearance in every position, including when swinging or reaching out from under it.

**Delivery work:** A knuckle boom is excluded from Subpart CC when delivering material to a construction site **only to transfer it from the truck to the ground, without arranging it in a particular sequence for hoisting** (§1926.1400(c)(17)). There are separate conditions for certain building supply deliveries. An excluded delivery **isn't automatically safe or free of other power line rules**. General industry work may fall under §1910.180, including its power line provisions in paragraph (j), depending on the crane.

**What's the line voltage, how high is it, what's your max reach straight up, and what's the job?** If you don't know the voltage, get it from the utility, and don't assume it's 50 kV or less.

- **Trigger distance:** Use **50 ft** wherever §1926.1407 or §1926.1408 says 20 ft. This substitution applies to lines over 350 kV and up to 1,000 kV (§1926.1409(a)).

  - **Option (2):** Maintain **50 ft** clearance, with the required encroachment prevention measures (§1926.1408(a)(2)(ii) and (b), with §1926.1409(a)).

**Tell the operator to stay in the cab unless there is an imminent danger of fire, explosion or another emergency that makes leaving necessary** (§1926.1408(g)(1)(i)(B)).

The employer must train **each operator and crew member** assigned to work with the equipment on the procedures for power line contact. This training must include (§1926.1408(g)(1)(i)(A)-(F)):

- **(A)** The electrocution danger if the operator touches the equipment and the ground at the same time.
- **(B)** Why staying in the cab matters to the operator's safety, with the emergency exception above.
- **(C)** The safest means of evacuating equipment that may be energized.
- **(D)** The danger of the potentially energized zone around the equipment (step potential).
- **(E)** The need for crew in the area to **not approach or touch the equipment or the load**.
- **(F)** Safe clearance distance from power lines.

Crew must also be trained to presume power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms the line has been and continues to be deenergized **and** it is visibly grounded at the worksite (§1926.1408(g)(1)(ii)).

**How to get out:** The regulation requires training on the safest means of evacuating, but the provision above doesn't specify a technique, such as how to jump or move away. I can't give you that step from these regulations. Get it from your employer's emergency procedure and training before the work starts.

This is the construction rule (Subpart CC). If your work is under general industry, check which Part 1910 requirements apply.

**Keep at least 6 ft** from the 13.8 kV line while traveling with no load (Table T, "over 0.75 to 50 kV"; §1926.1411(b)(2)). This applies to every part of the crane. Treat 6 ft as the minimum, not the target.

**Conditions under §1926.1411(b):**
- **Boom:** The boom and boom support system must be lowered enough to meet the clearance requirement (b)(1). "Boom down" counts only if it actually gives you that clearance.
- **Speed and terrain:** You must account for their effect on equipment movement, including boom movement and bounce (b)(3).

  - be positioned to effectively gauge the clearance
  - where necessary, use equipment that lets them communicate directly with the operator
  - give timely information so the required clearance is maintained
- **Night or poor visibility:** In addition to the above, you must illuminate the lines or identify their location by another means, **and** determine and use a safe path of travel (b)(5).

**If you're carrying a load**, Table T doesn't apply. Travel is then governed by §1926.1408, §1926.1409 or §1926.1410, as appropriate, and §1926.1417(u) (§1926.1411(a)).

response.text:
**In construction, you need a dedicated spotter if any part of the crane will get closer than 20 feet to a power line while traveling** (§1926.1411(b)(4)). An empty hook doesn't change that. If it'll be "close-ish," measured against that 20 feet, plan on a spotter.

**The spotter must** (§1926.1411(b)(4)):
- be in continuous contact with the driver/operator
- be positioned to effectively gauge the clearance
- where necessary, use equipment that lets them communicate directly with the operator
- give timely information so the required clearance is maintained

To count as a **dedicated spotter**, the person must meet the signal person qualifications in §1926.1428. Their **sole job** is watching the separation from the line and telling the operator what's needed to keep it (definition in §1926.1401).

**A spotter doesn't let you get any closer than these minimum clearances** (§1926.1411(b)(2), Table T):

| Line voltage | Minimum clearance while traveling |
|---|---|
| Up to 0.75 kV | 4 ft |
| Over 0.75 to 50 kV | 6 ft |
| Over 50 to 345 kV | 10 ft |
| Over 345 to 750 kV | 16 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 kV | 20 ft |
| Over 1,000 kV | Set by the utility owner/operator, or a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person for power transmission and distribution |

**You also have to:**
- Lower the boom/mast and its support system enough to meet these travel requirements (§1926.1411(b)(1)).
- Account for how speed and terrain affect the crane's movement, including boom/mast movement (§1926.1411(b)(3)). Bouncing or leaning can eat up clearance.
- **At night or in poor visibility**, in addition to the above, illuminate the lines or use another way to identify their location, **and** identify and use a safe path of travel (§1926.1411(b)(5)).

**Don't judge "pretty high" by eye.** Before moving, confirm the line voltage and make sure the line height and your crane's travel height leave enough clearance along the whole route.

This answer covers **construction travel with no load**. General industry work under §1910.180 has different rules.

**At 500 kV, keep at least 16 feet** while traveling with no load. This is the "over 345 to 750 kV" row of Table T (§1926.1411).

**Above 1,000 kV,** Table T gives no fixed distance. The clearance must be established by either the **utility owner/operator** or a **registered professional engineer who is a qualified person for electrical power transmission and distribution**. (Lines over 750 up to 1,000 kV require 20 feet.)

- **Boom/mast:** Lower the boom or mast and its support system enough to meet the paragraph's requirements.
- **Speed and terrain:** Account for their effect on equipment movement, including boom or mast movement.
- **Dedicated spotter:** One is required if any part of the equipment will get closer than **20 feet** to the line while traveling. For lines over 1,000 kV, this 20-foot spotter trigger doesn't replace the clearance set by the owner/operator or engineer.
- **Night or poor visibility:** You must also illuminate the lines or use another means of identifying their location, and identify and use a safe path of travel.

**With a load:** Table T doesn't apply. Under §1926.1411(a), travel on a construction site with a load is governed by §1926.1408, §1926.1409 or §1926.1410, as appropriate.

**It's allowed only as an exception.** Operating with any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) closer than the Table A distance to an energized line is **prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all of §1926.1410's requirements are met.** A GC's request doesn't satisfy any of them.

**The two threshold determinations**
1. **The work itself:** it's infeasible to do the work without breaching the Table A distance (§1926.1410(a)).
2. **The line:** after consulting the utility owner/operator, it's infeasible to **deenergize and ground** the line **or relocate** it (§1926.1410(b)).

If the work can be done outside the Table A distance, or the line can be deenergized and grounded or relocated, the exception isn't available.

**Passing those two isn't enough to start**
- **Minimum clearance distance:** the line owner/operator, or a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person for electrical power transmission and distribution, must set the distance needed to prevent contact under site conditions (§1926.1410(c)(1)). The factors include, but aren't limited to:
  - conditions affecting atmospheric conductivity
  - time needed to bring the equipment, load line and load (including rigging and lifting accessories) to a complete stop
  - wind
  - line sway
  - lighting
  - other conditions affecting the ability to prevent contact
- **Subpart V work:** the (c)(1) determination doesn't apply. The minimum approach distances the employer establishes under §1926.960(c)(1)(i) apply instead (§1926.1410(c)(2)).
- **Planning and the rest:** a planning meeting with the utility owner/operator or that qualified engineer is required to set the procedures (§1926.1410(d)). Those procedures and the remaining requirements of §1926.1410 must also be met.

**No. Table T in §1926.1411 is only for travel with no load.** §1926.1411(a) says travel with a load is governed by §1926.1408, §1926.1409 or §1926.1410, as appropriate, and §1926.1417(u).

**Going under the lines**

Under §1926.1408(d)(1), no part of the crane, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) may be below a power line unless your employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator **has de-energized it and visibly grounded it at the worksite**. The §1926.1408(d)(2) exceptions are:
- Work covered by Subpart V.
- **Non-extensible boom:** the uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom at true vertical, would be more than 20 ft below the plane of the line, or more than the Table A distance below it.
- **Articulating or extensible boom:** the same test, with the boom fully extended at true vertical.
- The employer demonstrates that compliance with (d)(1) is infeasible and meets §1926.1410.

For lines over 350 kV, §1926.1409 changes the distances used in §1926.1408.

**Clearance near energized lines (§1926.1408(a))**

Identify the work zone under (a)(1). If the equipment, load line or load could get within 20 ft at maximum working radius, use one option under (a)(2):
1. De-energize and visibly ground the line.
2. Keep 20 ft clearance.
3. Determine the voltage and keep the Table A clearance.

| Voltage (kV) | Table A minimum |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 | Set by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution |

For the 20 ft trigger and option 2, §1926.1409 substitutes **50 ft for lines over 350 kV up to 1,000 kV**. Over 1,000 kV, the utility owner/operator or such an engineer sets that distance.

These options don't by themselves permit going below a line; (d) still applies. Lines are presumed energized unless §1926.1408(e) is met.

**Options 2 and 3 also require (§1926.1408(b))**
- A planning meeting.
- Nonconductive tag lines, if tag lines are used.
- An elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs with high-visibility markings, in the operator's view, at 20 ft (adjusted per §1926.1409) or the Table A distance. If the operator can't see it, you must use a dedicated spotter as described in (b)(4)(ii).
- At least one (b)(4) measure: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, range control warning device, range limiting device, or insulating link/device.

**Pick and carry (§1926.1417(u))**
- Don't do it if the manufacturer prohibits it.
- A competent person must supervise, decide whether to reduce rated capacity, and make the safety determinations on load position, boom location, ground support, travel route, overhead obstructions and speed. Those determinations must be implemented.
- For equipment on tires, maintain the manufacturer's specified tire pressure.

To apply this to your move, check the line voltage, whether any part of the setup will pass below a line, your boom type, and the height of its uppermost part compared with the line. I can't determine your crane's travel limits or load ratings from these regulations.

**It depends on what you mean by "inside Table A."** This assumes construction work near an energized power line.

## If you're closer to the line than the Table A distance
**You must use the range limiter, and a spotter alone isn't enough.** If the equipment has a device that automatically limits range of movement, it must be used and set to prevent any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) from getting inside the **established minimum approach distance** (§1926.1410(d)(6)). A dedicated spotter is also required (§1926.1410(d)(2)).

These two items don't make the job legal by themselves. Work closer than Table A is allowed only if **all of §1926.1410** is met. That includes the employer showing that staying outside Table A is infeasible and that de-energizing and grounding is infeasible. It also includes the utility owner/operator or a qualified engineer setting the minimum approach distance, a planning meeting, and the other required protections.

## If you're working under Table A clearance, but staying at or beyond that distance
This is Option (3) in §1926.1408(a)(2)(iii). **A dedicated spotter can satisfy the "additional measure" requirement without the range limiter.** You need at least one of these (§1926.1408(b)(4)):
- proximity alarm
- dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator
- range control warning device
- range-limiting device
- insulating link

If the spotter is your chosen measure, the spotter must (§1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)):
- have a visual aid for identifying the minimum clearance distance
- be positioned to gauge that distance effectively
- use equipment to communicate directly with the operator where necessary
- give timely information so the clearance is maintained

A dedicated spotter must also meet the signal person qualifications in §1926.1428, and watching the separation must be their sole responsibility (§1926.1401, definition).

**The spotter doesn't replace the other measures** in §1926.1408(b)(1)–(3):
- a planning meeting
- non-conductive tag lines, if tag lines are used
- an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs, with the additional conditions in (b)(3)

This answer covers the OSHA rule only. I can't tell from these regulations whether the manufacturer, your employer or the site requires the limiter anyway.

**Will any part of the crane, load line or load need to get closer than the Table A distance?** If so, follow the first section.

**Yes. Because you're standing on the ground at the controls, the plan needs to address your own shock path.** If the boom or load line contacts or arcs to the line, the truck can become energized. My understanding is that §1926.1410(d) requires a ground-level remote operator to be protected by **either wireless controls that isolate you from the equipment or insulating mats that insulate you from the ground**. I'm working from memory and am not certain of the exact subparagraph or wording, so check the current text before work starts.

A belly box isn't necessarily wireless. If yours has a cable to the truck, don't treat it as isolating you. Even with a radio remote, stay clear of the truck, outriggers, load and rigging.

**Other minimum items in the §1926.1410(d) planning and procedures that affect you** (not the whole section):
- **Reclosers:** any automatic re-energizing device on the line must be made inoperative before work begins.
- **Dedicated spotter:** the spotter must be in continuous contact with you, positioned to judge clearance, and able to give you timely information.
- **Warning line or barricade:** this marks the minimum approach distance, with the conditions and exceptions in the rule.
- **Insulating link, nonconductive rigging and taglines:** these apply under the rule's conditions. The link has exceptions, and how it applies depends on your setup, such as whether you have a load line.
- **Range limiter:** if the crane has one, check how the rule and your plan require it to be used.
- **Grounding and access:** address equipment grounding, perimeter barricades (generally at least 10 ft from the equipment, or as far as feasible where space prevents that) and limiting access to essential employees.

- **Clearance:** know the minimum clearance distance in your plan. It must be set by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in power transmission and distribution (§1926.1410(c)).
- **Procedures and meeting:** the written procedures should be available on site, and you should be briefed on them.
- **Who's in charge:** know who is directing the plan and has authority to stop work. If the procedures aren't adequate, work must stop until they're fixed or the line is made safe.

I can't tell from these regulations whether your particular remote or mats give adequate isolation. Check the manufacturer's information and have the utility or qualified engineer address it in the plan.

- any other work subject to Subpart V.

**No, don't finish the lift as planned. Safely stop.** A lost spotter link and a plan that isn't working are both reasons to stop.

**Right now**
- **Stop safely.** If the ability to transmit signals is interrupted, the operator must safely stop operations requiring signals until it's restored and a proper signal is given and understood (§1926.1419(f)). This covers signal-person communication. A dedicated spotter has a separate continuous-contact requirement, below.
- **A dedicated spotter must stay in continuous contact with the operator.** The spotter must also be positioned to gauge clearance, use direct-communication equipment where necessary, and give timely information so the required distance is kept (§1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)). If you chose the spotter as your encroachment measure, you no longer have it. Another device on site doesn't make it OK to continue a plan that's failing.
- **The operator can stop and refuse to handle loads** whenever there's a safety concern, until a qualified person has determined that safety is assured (§1926.1418).

"Safely stop" doesn't mean making a rushed move or walking away from a suspended load. Don't move toward the lines. These provisions don't give a specific sequence for securing this load. Any movement needed to make it safe depends on the crane, load and site, and must not reduce the required clearance.

**Which rules apply before resuming**
- **At or outside the required clearance under §1926.1408:** Restore spotter contact and fix whatever isn't working. Review the line locations and prevention steps with the operator and the other workers in the area (§1926.1408(b)(1)). Keep the required warning line, barricade or signs, and at least one of the additional measures in §1926.1408(b)(4). The clearance depends on which option you're using under §1926.1408(a)(2), including Table A where applicable.
- **Working closer than Table A under §1926.1410:** This is allowed only if that section's conditions are met, including showing that staying at Table A distance is infeasible and consulting the utility owner/operator. If a problem arises in implementing the procedures, or shows they're inadequate to prevent electrocution, the employer must **safely stop operations** and either **develop new procedures** or have the utility **de-energize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line** before resuming (§1926.1410; I'm not certain of the paragraph letter).

**If the crane, load line or load has contacted a line, or may have,** treat it as an energized emergency and keep people away from the crane and load. Follow your site's electrical-contact procedures and get the utility and emergency services involved.

**Construction (Subpart CC): you can finish it during the shift, but it has to be started before the shift.** A **competent person** must *begin* a visual inspection before each shift the equipment will be used, and complete it before or during that shift (§1926.1412(d)(1)). Wire rope follows the same timing (§1926.1413(a)(1)).

**Some things can't wait:**
- **Level:** The equipment must be checked for level, within the manufacturer's tolerances, before each shift and after each move and setup (§1926.1412(d)(1)).
- **Safety devices:** The devices required by §1926.1415 must be in proper working order before operations begin. If one stops working during operations, the operator must safely stop (§1926.1415(b)).
- **Operational aids:** §1926.1416 also bars starting operations unless the listed aids are working, except where it allows temporary alternative measures (§1926.1416(d)).
- **Deficiencies:** If you find one in the shift inspection items, a competent person must immediately determine whether it's a safety hazard. If it is, the equipment must be taken out of service until it's corrected (§1926.1412(d), (f)). Wire rope has its own removal-from-service criteria (§1926.1413(a)(2) and (a)(4)).

**Who:** It must be a competent person. That means someone who can identify existing and predictable hazards and **has authority to take prompt corrective measures** (§1926.1401). The operator can do it if they meet that definition, but being the operator or holding a certification doesn't by itself make someone the competent person for this.

**General industry (Part 1910):** The timing and personnel rules are different. They're in §1910.179(j) for overhead and gantry cranes and §1910.180(d) for crawler, locomotive and truck cranes, so don't apply the construction timing there.

- **Shift inspection:** A competent person must begin a visual inspection before each shift the equipment will be used, and complete it before or during that shift. You don't have to boom down or take components apart **unless** the visual inspection or trial operation shows that further investigation requiring it is needed (§1926.1412(d)(1)).
- **Wire rope:** The shift visual inspection doesn't require booming down or untwisting (opening) the rope (§1926.1413(a)(1)). It covers apparent deficiencies, particularly in the ropes likely to be in use during the shift.

This answer doesn't cover other inspection types, such as monthly or annual, or any manufacturer requirements. If you're working under general industry rules (§1910.180) instead of construction, don't rely on the Subpart CC exception above.

**Yes.** If it has been **idle for 3 months or more**, a **qualified person** must inspect it **before initial use**, following the monthly inspection requirements (§1926.1412(h)). June to October can easily be over 3 months, so check the actual last-use date.

**Idle-equipment inspection**
- **Scope:** Monthly inspections cover the shift inspection items in §1926.1412(d) (see §1926.1412(e)(1)). These include control mechanisms, pressurized lines, hydraulic system and fluid level, hooks and latches, wire rope reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground conditions, level position and safety devices. Use the full list in (d)(1).
- **Deficiencies:** The equipment must not be used until the inspection shows that no corrective action under the shift inspection provisions is required (§1926.1412(e)(2), referring to (d)(3)). Safety devices and operational aids have their own rules (§§1926.1415 and 1926.1416).
- **Wire rope:** Include the monthly wire rope inspection (§1926.1413(b)).
- **Records:** For monthly inspections, record the items checked, the results, and the inspector's name and signature, plus the date. Keep the record at least 3 months (§1926.1412(e)(3)).

**Also check**
- **Annual inspection:** It must be done at least every 12 months by a qualified person (§1926.1412(f)). If it's due, complete it before use. The idle-equipment inspection doesn't replace it. The annual wire rope inspection is under §1926.1413(c).
- **Assembly:** If it's assembled for this job, a qualified person must do a post-assembly inspection after assembly and before use (§1926.1412(c)).
- **Repairs or modifications:** Any done during the layup may trigger inspection before use (§1926.1412(a)-(b)). Modifications also have approval requirements (§1926.1434).
- **Shift inspection:** A competent person must begin one before each shift, and complete it before or during that shift (§1926.1412(d)(1)).
- **Job site:** Before use, address ground conditions (§1926.1402) and power line safety (§§1926.1407-.1411, as applicable to assembly and operation). Make sure the operator meets the training, certification and evaluation requirements (§1926.1427).

Also follow the manufacturer's procedures where Subpart CC requires them. I can't tell you from these regulations what the manufacturer calls for after storage, such as fluids, batteries or lubrication, so check the manual.

**Under construction rules (§1926.1412(b)(1)), a qualified person must inspect the crane after the brake repair is completed and before initial use.** A braking system repair that relates to safe operation is covered. If manufacturer criteria are inapplicable or unavailable, §1926.1412(b)(1)(ii) requires the following:

1. **Decide whether a registered professional engineer (RPE) is needed** to develop criteria for the repair.
   - If an RPE isn't needed, the employer must ensure the **qualified person** develops the criteria.
   - If an RPE is needed, the employer must ensure an **RPE** develops them.
2. **Determine whether the repair meets those criteria.**

**Return to service:** Under §1926.1412(b)(2), the crane must not be used until the inspection shows that the repair meets the applicable criteria.

This answer applies to construction work under Subpart CC. It doesn't cover requirements for general industry work under Part 1910.

**Who:** a **qualified person** must inspect the crane once assembly is complete (§1926.1412(c)(1); §1926.1404(f) points to this inspection). Under §1926.1401, that means someone who, by a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, or by extensive knowledge, training and experience, has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve problems relating to the subject matter. Pinning the boom or running the assembly doesn't by itself make someone qualified for this inspection.

**Checked against:** the **manufacturer's equipment criteria**, to assure the crane is configured in accordance with them (§1926.1412(c)(1)).

**If manufacturer criteria are unavailable** (§1926.1412(c)(2)), the qualified person must determine whether a **registered professional engineer (RPE)** familiar with that type of equipment is needed to develop the configuration criteria:
- **RPE not needed:** the employer must ensure the qualified person develops them.
- **RPE needed:** the employer must ensure the RPE develops them.

**Before the first pick:** the crane **must not be used** until this inspection demonstrates that it's configured according to the applicable criteria (§1926.1412(c)(3)).

**Signature:** §1926.1412(c) doesn't spell out a signed form or written record for the post-assembly inspection. Your employer, the site or the manufacturer may require one.

**Shift inspection:** a **competent person** must also begin a visual inspection before each shift the crane will be used, and complete it before or during that shift (§1926.1412(d)(1)). Don't treat it as a substitute for the post-assembly inspection.

I can't give you the boom pin, section sequence or configuration specifics for your crane from these regulations. Get those from the manufacturer's procedures.
