**No. The trainee can't operate in that setup.** For lines up to 350 kV, an operator-in-training is barred if any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) could get **within 20 ft** of the line when operated up to maximum working radius in the work zone (§1926.1427(b)). At about 15 ft, you're inside that. Having a trainer or spotter doesn't lift the ban, and the 10 ft Table A distance doesn't replace the 20 ft trainee limit.

**Work zone:** It's either (§1926.1408(a)(1)):
- an area marked by boundaries (such as flags or a range limiting or range control warning device), where the operator is prohibited from operating past them, or
- the full 360° around the crane, up to maximum working radius.

If you set up the crane or boundaries so that nothing could get within 20 ft at maximum working radius **in that zone**, this power line ban wouldn't be triggered. Check this before he operates, including load size, rigging and tag lines. The other trainee requirements, including continuous monitoring by a qualified trainer, still apply (§1926.1427(b)).

**For a qualified operator:** Being within 20 ft requires one of these options (§1926.1408(a)(2)):
1. **De-energize and ground:** The utility owner/operator confirms the line is de-energized, and it's visibly grounded at the worksite.
2. **20 ft clearance:** Nothing gets closer than 20 ft, using the §1926.1408(b) measures.
3. **Table A clearance:** Get the voltage from the utility owner/operator. For lines up to 50 kV, the minimum is **10 ft**. The §1926.1408(b) measures also apply. Don't rely on an assumed 13.8 kV.

**§1926.1408(b) measures for options 2 and 3:**
- Hold a planning meeting with the operator and the other workers who will be in the area of the equipment or load.
- Use non-conductive tag lines, if tag lines are used.
- Erect and maintain an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs with flags or similar high-visibility markings at the required distance. If the operator can't see it, use a dedicated spotter.
- Add at least one of these: a proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, range control warning device, range limiting device or insulating link/device.

Presume the line is energized unless the utility confirms it's de-energized and it's visibly grounded (§1926.1408(e)). Work under or near the line has further requirements in §1926.1408.

This assumes construction work under Subpart CC and doesn't cover any stricter state, utility or site rules.

**Certification isn't required under the federal construction rule, but training is.** This applies to equipment with a **maximum manufacturer-rated capacity of 2,000 lbs or less** (§1926.1441; see also the exception in §1926.1427(a)).

- **Operators:** Before they run it, you must train each one on the safe operation of the **type of equipment** they'll be using (§1926.1441(e)).
- **Signal persons:** You must train them in the proper use of the signals that apply to this equipment (§1926.1441(f)).

**Other rules still apply.** The small size doesn't exempt you from the rest of §1926.1441. It includes requirements on assembly/disassembly, operating procedures, safety devices and operational aids, and keeping clear of the load. It also makes other Subpart CC provisions apply, including power line safety. Check the full section before you put the picker to work.

**What this answer assumes:**
- **Capacity:** The manufacturer's maximum rating is 2,000 lbs or less. A bigger crane doesn't qualify just because you limit your lifts to 2,000 lbs or it's set up in a lower-capacity configuration.
- **Type of work:** You're doing construction and the picker is equipment covered by Subpart CC (§1926.1400). General industry work, such as plant or shop operations, falls under Part 1910, and this exemption doesn't answer what's required there.
- **Other requirements:** This covers federal OSHA only. I can't tell you from these regulations whether your state plan, local licensing, customer or site requires more.

What kind of picker is it, and what work are you using it for?

response.text:
**If it's operator certification that OSHA requires for your construction work and you're already an employee, then no.** Your employer has to provide it at no cost to you. This is in §1926.1427; I believe it's paragraph (a)(4), but check the paragraph number against the current text.

It depends on a few things:

- **Type of work:** The rule covers construction under Subpart CC. I know of no similar card-cost requirement for general industry work in §1910.179 or §1910.180.
- **Equipment:** Operator certification isn't required for derricks, sideboom cranes, or equipment with a maximum manufacturer-rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 lb or less (§1926.1427(a); see also §§1926.1436(q), 1926.1440(a) and 1926.1441(a)).
- **Type of card:** For signal persons (§1926.1428) and riggers who must be qualified (e.g., §1926.1425(c)), Subpart CC doesn't require a "crane card" as such. The operator certification cost rule doesn't automatically cover a card for those roles. Required *training* under Subpart CC is a separate matter (§1926.1430).
- **Your status:** The no-cost duty is owed to employees. A card you got on your own before being hired is a different situation, and this rule doesn't by itself establish that you'd be reimbursed.

A certification also doesn't replace your employer's duty to evaluate you on the equipment (§1926.1427(f)).

I can't answer from these regulations whether state law, a union agreement or a repayment agreement affects your costs. State or local operator licensing also has its own conditions under §1926.1427.

**What's the card for (operator, rigger or signal person), what equipment is it, and is the work construction?** With that, you'll know which of these applies to you.

| | Accredited testing organization (§1926.1427(d)) | Audited employer program (§1926.1427(e)) |
|---|---|---|
| **Goes with you to a new company?** | **Yes.** It is portable. | **No.** It is not portable and counts only while your employer is the one that issued it. |
| **How long it's good for** | **5 years** | **5 years**, but leaving that employer ends your ability to rely on it, even with time left. |

**If you only have your old company's in-house certification:** your new employer can't use it to meet the certification requirement. For equipment that requires certification, you need another valid route, such as an accredited certification, the new employer's own qualifying audited program, or a state or local license where that applies (§1926.1427(c)–(e)). Until then, you can operate only as an operator-in-training, under the supervision and other conditions in §1926.1427(a) and (b).

**An accredited certification isn't enough by itself.** Your new employer must also **evaluate** you before letting you operate on your own (§1926.1427(a) and (f)). The evaluation covers whether you have the skills, knowledge and judgment to run the equipment safely, including for the specific configuration and tasks, such as blind lifts or multi-crane lifts. Your old employer's evaluation doesn't replace it. The certification must also cover the type of crane you'll be running.

**Other cases:**
- **State or local license:** where a qualifying government license is required, its validity and conditions depend on that program. It applies only within that government's jurisdiction, and the federal criteria limit it to no more than 5 years (§1926.1427(c)).
- **Exceptions:** derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment with a maximum manufacturer-rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less are excluded from §1926.1427's certification requirement (§1926.1427(a)). Other qualification or training rules can still apply.

This answer covers construction work under Subpart CC. U.S. military qualifications and state-plan or local requirements may differ, so check those if they apply to you.

These rules apply to an **audited employer program** under §1926.1427(e).

**Audit timing (§1926.1427(e)(4))**
- **First audit:** within **3 months** of the beginning of the program.
- **After that:** at least **every 3 years**.

**If the auditor finds a significant deficiency (§1926.1427(e)(6))**
- **Qualifications stop:** no operator may be qualified until the auditor confirms the deficiency has been corrected.
- **Follow-up audit:** the program must be audited again **within 180 days** of that confirmation.
- **Report to OSHA:** the auditor must file a documented report of the deficiency with the appropriate **OSHA Regional Office within 15 days** of determining that it exists.
- **Records:** the employer must keep records of the audits for **3 years** and make them available to OSHA on request. I'm less sure of the sub-paragraph number for this requirement, so check it within §1926.1427(e).

The pause above is on qualifying operators. I wouldn't read it as either automatically canceling or protecting earlier qualifications. If the finding calls earlier test results into question, get that specific situation reviewed.

**Also check as you set it up (§1926.1427(e))**
- **Auditor:** must be certified by an accredited crane operator testing organization to evaluate the tests, and **must not be your employee**.
- **Tests:** written and practical tests must be developed by an accredited testing organization or approved by the auditor under nationally recognized test development criteria. Their administration must also meet the paragraph's auditor-approval requirements.
- **Portability:** qualification under your program isn't portable. It counts only while the operator is employed by, and operating equipment for, your company.
- **State or local licensing:** where a government license meeting the federal criteria is required, your in-house program doesn't replace it (§1926.1427(c)).
- **Employer evaluation:** certification through your program doesn't replace the separate operator evaluation (§1926.1427(f)).

response.text:
**Under §1926.1427(f)(6), the employer must document that the evaluation was completed. The document must show:**
1. The operator's name
2. The evaluator's name **and signature**
3. The date
4. The **make, model and configuration** of the equipment used in the evaluation

**Availability:** It must be available at the worksite for as long as the employer employs the operator (§1926.1427(f)(6)).

**Operators employed before December 10, 2018:** The employer may rely on its previous assessments instead of newly evaluating their existing knowledge and skills (§1926.1427(f)(2)). In that case, the document must show (§1926.1427(f)(6)):
- The date of the employer's determination of the operator's abilities
- The make, model and configuration of equipment on which the operator previously demonstrated competency

**Related requirements for the evaluation itself:**
- **What it covers:** The operator must demonstrate the skills, knowledge and ability to recognize and avert risk needed to operate the equipment safely. This includes its safety devices, operational aids, software, size and configuration. The operator must also demonstrate the ability to do the assigned hoisting work, such as blind lifts, personnel hoisting or multi-crane lifts, if applicable (§1926.1427(f)(1)).
- **Certificates:** A certificate or degree alone doesn't qualify an operator under the evaluation requirement (§1926.1427(f)(3)).
- **Evaluator:** This person must have the knowledge, training and experience needed to assess equipment operators (§1926.1427(f)(4)), and must be an employee or agent of the employer. The employer remains responsible if it uses an agent (§1926.1427(f)(5)).
- **Other equipment:** After a successful evaluation, the operator may run other equipment if the employer can demonstrate it doesn't require substantially different skills, knowledge or risk-recognition ability (§1926.1427(f)(5)).
- **Retraining:** When retraining is required under §1926.1427(b)(5), the employer must re-evaluate the operator on the retraining subject (§1926.1427(f)(7)).

This answer covers construction work under Subpart CC.

response.text:
**No. The new employer can't use your old company's evaluation to qualify you** under the construction crane rule, if the evaluator was your last company's own (employer's) qualified evaluator. §1926.1428(a)(2) says that assessment is **not portable**, and other employers may not use it to meet the section's requirements.

**Before you give any signals**, the new employer must make sure you meet the qualification requirements through one of these (§1926.1428(a)):
- **Third-party qualified evaluator (a)(1):** You have documentation from that evaluator showing you meet the requirements.
- **Employer's qualified evaluator (a)(2):** The new employer's evaluator assesses you, determines that you meet the requirements, and provides documentation.

**Documentation (a)(3):** The employer must make it available at the site while you're employed there. It must specify each type of signaling you're qualified for, such as hand or radio signals.

**What you must meet (§1926.1428(c)):**
- Know and understand the type of signals used. For hand signals, this includes the Standard Method.
- Be competent in using those signals.
- Have a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including the crane dynamics of swinging and stopping loads and boom deflection from hoisting.
- Know and understand the relevant requirements of §§1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and §1926.1428.
- Show all of this through an oral or written test **and** a practical test.

**If your old evaluator was actually an independent third party**, not your former company's evaluator, the non-portability sentence in (a)(2) doesn't apply. Check who issued your documentation and in what capacity. Even with third-party documentation, if your later actions show you don't meet the requirements, the employer must stop you from signaling until you've been retrained and reassessed (§1926.1428(b)).

This answer covers construction work under Subpart CC.

response.text:
**No, not on certification alone.** In construction, he must be **trained, certified or licensed, and evaluated** before operating it on his own (§1926.1427(a)). The exceptions in §1926.1427(a), such as operators-in-training, don't make certification a substitute for your evaluation.

**Before he operates it independently:**
- **Certification:** Confirm it's valid and covers this crane's type (and capacity, if the certification specifies it) (§1926.1427(d)). Accredited certification is valid for 5 years. If a state or local license that meets OSHA's criteria is required where you're working, he needs that too (§1926.1427(c) and (e)).
- **Your evaluation:** He must demonstrate the following (§1926.1427(f)(1)):
  - The skills, knowledge, and ability to recognize and avert risk needed to operate the equipment safely. This includes its safety devices, operational aids, software, size and configuration. **The luffing jib has to be covered**, as do factors such as lifting capacity, boom length, attachments and counterweight setup.
  - The ability to do the assigned hoisting work, including blind lifts, personnel hoisting and multi-crane lifts if applicable.
- **Evaluator:** This must be someone with the knowledge, training and experience to assess operators (§1926.1427(f)). The evaluator must be your employee or agent. Using a third-party agent doesn't remove your responsibility.
- **Documentation:** Record his name, the evaluator's name and signature, the date, and the **make, model and configuration** of the equipment used. Keep it available at the worksite while he's employed by you (§1926.1427(f)).

**Testing:** He must show he meets the requirements below through **both an oral or written test and a practical test** (§1926.1428(c)(5)). He must:
- Know and understand the type of signals used. For hand signals, this includes the Standard Method (§1926.1428(c)(1)).
- Be competent in applying that type of signal (§1926.1428(c)(2)).
- Have a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including the crane dynamics of swinging and stopping loads and boom deflection from hoisting loads (§1926.1428(c)(3)).
- Know and understand the relevant requirements of §§1926.1419–1926.1422 and §1926.1428 (§1926.1428(c)(4)).

**Who can assess him:** He must be qualified **before giving any signals**, by one of these (§1926.1428(a)):
1. **Third-party qualified evaluator:** He has documentation from that evaluator showing he meets the requirements (§1926.1428(a)(1)).
2. **Employer's qualified evaluator:** The evaluator assesses him, determines that he meets the requirements, and the employer documents it (§1926.1428(a)(2)). This assessment **isn't portable**, so other employers can't use it.

A qualified evaluator must have demonstrated competence in accurately assessing signal persons. A third-party evaluator is an entity that has demonstrated this through its independence and expertise. An employer's evaluator is a person employed by the signal person's employer (§1926.1401).

**On site:** The employer must make the documentation available at the site while the signal person is employed by that employer (§1926.1428(a)(3)).

**Requalification:** If his later actions show he doesn't meet the requirements, the employer must stop him from working as a signal person until he's retrained and reassessed and found to meet them (§1926.1428(b)).

**Yes to both,** for construction work under Subpart CC.

**Retraining: §1926.1430(g)(2)**
The employer must provide refresher training in relevant topics when the employee's **conduct**, or an evaluation of their knowledge, indicates that retraining is necessary. It is triggered by that indication, so finishing training last year doesn't satisfy it.

Repeatedly standing in a hazardous part of the swing radius is conduct that points to a need for retraining. Relevant topics include:
- **Struck-by and pinch/crush hazards:** Employees assigned to work on or near the equipment must be trained to recognize the hazard areas posed by the rotating superstructure (§1926.1424(a)(2)(i)).
- **Keeping clear:** Employees who work with the equipment must be instructed to keep clear of holes and crush/pinch points, and on the hazards in §1926.1424 (§1926.1430(e)).

**Checking understanding: §1926.1430(g)(1)**
The employer must **evaluate each employee required to be trained under Subpart CC to confirm that they understand the training.** Attendance or a completion record alone doesn't show this. The paragraphs cited here don't prescribe a test format. Since refresher training is also training under this subpart, I read (g)(1) as applying to it too.

**Retraining isn't the only duty**
Check the work area controls in §1926.1424(a). Where accessible areas pose a reasonably foreseeable risk of an employee being struck or pinched/crushed by the rotating superstructure, the employer must address that hazard. This includes marking the boundaries with control lines, warning lines, railings or similar barriers, subject to the rule's conditions and alternative for when that is infeasible (§1926.1424(a)(2)(ii)).

If the rigger has to enter a hazard area for assigned work and will be out of the operator's view, there are also requirements for notifying and coordinating with the operator (§1926.1424(a)(3)). Don't wait for retraining to correct a current exposure.

This answer covers construction. If the work is general industry under Part 1910, don't assume these Subpart CC training provisions apply.

**You can use short-set outriggers only if the manufacturer permits that setup.** When the load and radius require outriggers, or you use them for assembly or disassembly, they must be **fully extended or, if the manufacturer's procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart** (§1926.1404(q)(1)).

**Load chart**
- Use only a deployment that the chart and manufacturer's procedures allow, with the capacity for that setup. Don't apply full-extension capacities to a short-set crane.
- If they don't permit your position, you can't use it for a lift that requires outriggers. Don't estimate or derate your own way to a number. Change the setup, location or lift plan within what the manufacturer allows.
- Don't exceed rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)(1)). Verify the load weight as §1926.1417(o)(3) requires.
- Follow the manufacturer's operating procedures (§1926.1417(a)). Load charts and procedures must be readily available in the cab (§1926.1417(c)).

**Setting up** (§1926.1404(q))
- Set the outriggers to remove the equipment weight from the wheels (locomotive cranes are excepted).
- Floats, if used, must be attached to the outriggers.
- The operator or a signal person must be able to see each outrigger during extension and setting.
- Blocking must:
  - be strong enough to prevent crushing, bending or shear failure
  - be thick, wide and long enough to completely support the float, transmit the load to the ground and maintain stability
  - go only under the outer bearing surface of the extended outrigger beam

**Ground and tight-site issues**
- The ground must be firm, drained and graded enough that, with supporting materials if needed, the manufacturer's specifications for **support and level** are met (§1926.1402(b)). The controlling entity has ground-preparation and hazard-information duties (§1926.1402(c)). If conditions fall short, see §1926.1402(e) for the required discussion with that entity.
- Guard against workers being struck or caught by the rotating superstructure, including marking and barricading the swing hazard area (§1926.1424(a)).
- If there's a safety concern, the operator has authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person determines safety is assured (§1926.1418).

**Written exam** (§1926.1427(j))
The topics tied to this question include operating and performance characteristics, using and calculating load/capacity information for various configurations, and the suitability of the supporting ground to handle expected loads. They also include site hazards, Subpart CC and the applicable Appendix C subjects.

**Not covered by these regulations:** whether your RT allows intermediate or mixed outrigger positions, its capacities and working areas in each one, and any pinning, programming or capacity-limiter settings. Check that crane's load chart and manual. I also can't tell you how a particular testing organization words its exam questions.

**Not just because it's faster.** Under **§1926.1431(a)**, using equipment to hoist employees is prohibited unless **the employer demonstrates** that erecting, using and dismantling conventional means of access (such as a personnel hoist, ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform or scaffold):

- **would be more hazardous**, or
- **isn't possible** because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions.

Speed, cost and convenience don't meet that test. It also isn't enough to rule out scaffolding if another conventional method, such as an aerial lift, would work without being more hazardous.

**Limited exceptions:** §1926.1431(a) doesn't apply to work covered by Subpart R (steel erection). Subpart R has its own provisions, so this isn't a blanket OK. §1926.1431 also treats certain specialized operations differently, such as some pile driving work. If either might apply, tell me the task.

**If the test is met**, the rest of §1926.1431 still applies. Key requirements include:

- **Setup:** The crane must be uncrated or unpacked as needed, **level within 1%** of grade, and on footing firm enough to keep it that way. Outriggers or stabilizers, if used, must be set according to the load chart and manufacturer's procedures (§1926.1431(c)).
- **Capacity:** The total load, including the hoisted platform, people, materials and rigging, generally **must not exceed 50% of rated capacity** for that radius and configuration (§1926.1431(d)).
- **Platform and rigging:** They must meet the design, loading and attachment criteria. Not just any basket will do (§1926.1431(e)–(g)).
- **Before lifting people:** A trial lift, inspection and proof test at **125%** of the platform's rated capacity are required, under the conditions in §1926.1431.
- **Work practices and pre-lift meeting:** Requirements for these, including fall protection and communication, are also in §1926.1431.

**What to ask your super:** "What makes scaffold, a lift or other conventional access more hazardous or impossible here?" If the only answer is "it takes longer," §1926.1431(a) doesn't allow the man basket, unless one of the exceptions above applies.

**OSHA's regulations don't publish the exam questions or a list of tested electrical devices.** For certification, the written test must cover procedures for preventing and responding to power line contact, and knowledge of Subpart CC (§1926.1427(j)(1)(i)). Appendix C also includes power line hazards and safe operation near lines. I can't tell you how a particular testing organization, state or city weights these. These are the Subpart CC items to study:

**Work zone and clearance**
- First identify the work zone and whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get within 20 ft of a line. If so, use one of three options (§1926.1408(a)):
  - Deenergize and **visibly ground** the line at the worksite, as confirmed by the utility.
  - Keep **20 ft** clearance.
  - Get the voltage and use **Table A**.

| Voltage (kV) | Table A minimum distance |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 | Set by the utility/owner or a qualified registered PE |

- For lines over 350 kV, 50 ft replaces the 20 ft trigger. Over 1,000 kV, the utility/owner or PE sets that distance (§1926.1409).

**Encroachment prevention (§1926.1408(b))**
- This applies under the 20 ft and Table A options.
- You need a planning meeting, and any tag lines must be nonconductive.
- You also need at least one of these: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, range control warning device, range limiting device, or insulating link/device. An elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs also counts.
- **Assembly/disassembly** has its own rules and list of measures (§1926.1407).

**Working closer than Table A (§1926.1410)**

This is allowed only under strict conditions, including:
- The employer shows that staying at Table A distance is infeasible, and the utility/owner determines that deenergizing and grounding, or relocating the line, is infeasible.
- The utility/owner or a qualified PE sets the minimum distance and procedures.
- Automatic reclosing is made inoperative if the device allows it.
- A dedicated spotter and an elevated warning line or barricade are used.
- An insulating link/device is installed between the load line and load, subject to the rule's limited exceptions.
- Rigging is nonconductive if it may get within the Table A distance, and any tag lines are nonconductive.
- The crane is properly grounded.
- Any range limiter the crane has is used.
- Insulating line hose or cover-up is installed by the utility/owner, unless unavailable for that voltage.
- Barricades are at least 10 ft from the equipment where feasible, and access is limited.

**Operator and crew training (§1926.1408(g))**
- **Contact response:** Stay in the cab unless there's imminent danger of fire, explosion or another emergency that requires leaving.
- **Evacuation:** Know the safest way out, the danger of touching the equipment and ground at the same time, and the energized zone around the crane. Others must not approach or touch the equipment.
- **Line status:** Presume lines are energized and uninsulated unless the rule's conditions for treating them otherwise are met (see also §1926.1408(e)).
- **Device limits:** Know the limitations of insulating links, proximity alarms and range control devices.
- **Grounding:** Know how to ground the equipment properly and the limits of grounding.

**Also review:** work below power lines (§1926.1408(d)), work near transmitter/communication towers (§1926.1408(f)), and travel under or near lines with no load (§1926.1411).

**The crane must be uniformly level, within 1% of level grade** (§1926.1431(c)(1)). That's 1 ft of rise or fall in 100 ft, or about 0.57°. It's **not** 1 degree.

Setup also requires:
- **Footing:** A qualified person must determine that it's sufficiently firm and stable (§1926.1431(c)(1)).
- **Outriggers or stabilizers:** If the crane has them, all must be extended and locked. All must be extended the same amount, in line with the manufacturer's procedures and load charts (§1926.1431(c)(2)).

This is the construction rule. Being level doesn't by itself clear you for the lift: the other requirements in §1926.1431 also apply. These include first showing that conventional ways of reaching the work are more hazardous or not possible (§1926.1431(a)). If the manufacturer sets a tighter level tolerance, check its procedures; I can't tell you that from these regulations.

**No.** Not for a personnel lift, even if the load chart allows unequal or short-jacked outriggers for ordinary lifts. Under **§1926.1431(c)(2)**, with outriggers or stabilizers:

- **All** of them must be extended and locked.
- The extension must be the **same for all** of them.
- The extension must also follow the manufacturer's procedures and load chart.

So you can't pull in only the tight side. An equal, reduced extension on **all** outriggers can meet this rule only if the manufacturer's procedures and load chart permit that position. Use the chart for that exact configuration. I can't tell you whether your crane has one.

- **Level and footing:** The crane must be uniformly level within **1% of level grade**, on footing a qualified person has determined is sufficiently firm and stable (**§1926.1431(c)(1)**).
- **Capacity:** The total load (platform, rigging, people, tools, materials and anything else counted as load) must not exceed **50% of rated capacity** for the radius and configuration, except during proof testing (**§1926.1431**).

If equal extension won't fit with a permitted chart and adequate capacity, don't make the lift from that setup. Look at another crane position, a different crane or another way to access the work.

**Equipment limit:** The total load, meaning the loaded platform plus rigging, **must not exceed 50% of the equipment's rated capacity** for the radius and configuration in use. The exception is during proof testing (§1926.1431(d)(1)).

**What to count:**
- The platform itself
- Occupants
- Their tools and materials
- The rigging
- Load-attaching equipment such as the load block, ropes, slings, shackles and other ancillary attachments (see the definition of "load" in §1926.1401)

For deductions specific to your crane, such as hook blocks, stowed jibs or load line weight, check the manufacturer's load chart and its notes. I can't determine those from these regulations.

**Platform limit (a separate check, §1926.1431(f)):**
- The platform must not be loaded beyond its rated load capacity.
- It may carry only employees, their tools and the materials needed to do their work. It must not be used to hoist materials or tools when it isn't hoisting personnel.
- Materials and tools must be secured and evenly distributed while the platform is suspended.
- The number of occupants must not exceed the number required for the work or the number the platform was designed to hold.

**Both limits must be met.** Being within the platform's rating doesn't show you're within the crane's 50% limit, and the reverse is also true.

response.text:
**It's every shift, not just every day.** This assumes "basket" means a personnel platform hoisted by a crane in construction.

| Situation | New trial lift? |
|---|---|
| Each shift in which people will be hoisted | **Yes**, immediately before the shift (§1926.1431(h)(2)). Two such shifts in a day need two trial lifts. |
| Crane moved and set up in a new location | **Yes**, before hoisting employees (§1926.1431(h)(2)(i)). |
| Crane returned to a previously used location | **Yes**, even if you trial lifted there earlier (§1926.1431(h)(2)(i)). So redo it on the other side of the building, and again when you come back and set up, before hoisting anyone at either spot. |
| Lift route changed | **Yes, unless** the competent person determines the new route presents no new factors affecting safety (§1926.1431(h)(2)(ii)). This exception is for route changes, not for moving the crane. |

**How to do it (§1926.1431(h)(1)):**
- The platform is **unoccupied** and loaded to **at least the anticipated liftweight**.
- Lift from ground level, or wherever employees will get in, to **each location** where the platform will be hoisted and positioned.
- For several locations from one setup, you can do separate trial lifts or one sequential trial lift. It must match the method you'll use with people aboard.

**Competent person checks:**
- **During the trial lift (§1926.1431(h)(3)):**
  - Required safety devices and operational aids are activated and working, and others meet §§1926.1415 and 1926.1416.
  - Nothing interferes with the crane or platform.
  - The lift won't exceed **50% of rated capacity** at any time.
  - The load radius has been accurately determined.
- **Immediately afterward (§1926.1431(h)(4)):** Visually inspect the crane, base support or ground, and platform for defects, problems or adverse effects. Confirm the test weight has been removed.

**Before each lift with people (§1926.1431(h)(5)):** Hoist the platform a few inches with the people, materials and tools aboard, and check that it's secure and properly balanced. The other pre-lift checks in that paragraph also apply. Any condition that fails the requirements must be corrected before hoisting personnel (§1926.1431(h)(6)).

**The proof test is separate.** It's required at each jobsite before hoisting personnel on the platform, and after any repair or modification (§1926.1431(g)). A trial lift doesn't replace it.

**Yes, you can do the proof test at the same time as the trial lift** (§1926.1431(j)).

- **Weight:** 125% of the **platform's rated capacity**, not 125% of what you plan to carry. For example, a 1,000 lb rated platform needs a 1,250 lb test load.
- **Time:** Hold it suspended for **5 minutes** with the test load evenly distributed.
- **When:** At each jobsite before hoisting anyone on the platform, and after any repair or modification.
- **What's tested:** The platform and rigging together.
- **After the test:** A competent person must inspect the platform and rigging. If there are deficiencies, correct them and repeat the proof test before hoisting personnel.

These are in §1926.1431(j).

**If you combine them,** you still have to meet all the trial lift and inspection requirements in §1926.1431(h). Passing the proof test doesn't replace them, and later trial lifts may be required even when a new proof test isn't, such as before each shift.

These are the construction rules under Subpart CC.

**No, not at 40 feet, unless the work is covered by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart V** (electric power transmission and distribution).

- **The rule:** Hoisting personnel is prohibited within **50 feet of a power line over 350 kV** (20 feet for lines up to 350 kV), except for work covered by Subpart V (§1926.1431(s)). At 500 kV and 40 feet, you're inside that distance.
- **Don't use the 25-foot figure:** Table A in §1926.1408 gives 25 feet for lines over 350 kV through 500 kV. That is an equipment clearance under the power line rules. It doesn't shorten the 50-foot limit for hoisting personnel.
- **Subpart V exception:** Being a general contractor rather than a utility doesn't settle this by itself. The exception depends on whether the **work** is covered by Subpart V. If your job is general construction that just happens to be near the line, don't assume it qualifies. I can't determine Subpart V coverage or its requirements from the regulations I'm limited to.
- **De-energizing:** Under §1926.1408(a)(2)(i), the utility owner/operator must confirm the line is de-energized, and it must be visibly grounded at the worksite. That option addresses the §1926.1408 encroachment precautions. I can't point to wording in it that expressly lifts the §1926.1431(s) personnel hoisting limit, so get that resolved before relying on it.

**If you move the work so the hoisting stays at least 50 feet away:**
- **Justify the basket:** You may use it only if conventional means of reaching the work (such as a ladder, stairway, aerial lift, elevating work platform or scaffold) would be more hazardous, or aren't possible because of the project's structural design or worksite conditions (§1926.1431(a)). Convenience isn't enough. All other applicable requirements of §1926.1431 also apply.
- **Check the whole work zone:** For lines over 350 kV up to 1,000 kV, **50 feet replaces 20 feet** in §§1926.1407 and 1926.1408 (§1926.1409). Identify the work zone and determine whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get within 50 feet. If you don't use demarcated boundaries, assess 360 degrees around the equipment out to its maximum working radius (§1926.1408(a)(1)). If it could, the §1926.1408(a)(2) requirements apply, even if the planned basket position is farther away.
- **Assembly and disassembly:** Check these separately under §1926.1407, with the same 50-foot substitution.

**Before planning further,** confirm the line voltage with the utility owner/operator and measure the closest distance the hoisting operation could reach, including boom movement and basket drift. The 40 feet to the planned work location may not be the closest approach.

**Not just on the judgment that there's no better way.** Hoisting employees while the crane travels is prohibited, even at a creep. For a rough terrain crane, the relevant exception is where **the employer demonstrates there is no less hazardous way to do the work** (§1926.1431(l)(1)). The other exception is for equipment on fixed rails.

**If the employer can demonstrate that, all of these apply (§1926.1431(l)(2)):**
- Travel is restricted to a **fixed track or runway**. Being on a slab doesn't by itself establish a runway.
- Travel is limited to the **load radius of the boom used during the lift**. Check the distance to the next bay against this.
- The **boom is parallel to the direction of travel**, unless the employer demonstrates another position is safer.
- A **complete trial run** along the route is done before anyone gets in the platform. It can be done during the trial lift.
- On rubber tires, **tire condition and air pressure** are checked. The **on-rubber chart capacity** applies, and the **50% reduction** for personnel hoisting still applies. Outriggers may be partially retracted as necessary for travel.

**The other personnel hoisting rules still apply, including:**
- Hoisting people with the crane at all is allowed only if conventional access would be **more hazardous or isn't possible** because of the structure's design or worksite conditions (§1926.1431(a)). That is a separate showing from the one for travel.
- The rest of §1926.1431 covers level and footing, capacity, platform, fall protection, trial lift, inspection and the pre-lift meeting. §1926.1431 is supplemental to the rest of Subpart CC, so power line and other requirements apply too.

**Right now:** don't move with them in the basket unless the employer has made both showings and every condition above is met. Otherwise, land the platform, get everyone out, reposition and set up again. Before the next hoist, do a new trial lift for the new location (§1926.1431(h)).

I can't tell from these regulations whether your crane may pick and carry in this configuration, or what its on-rubber capacity, speed or tire pressure limits are. Check the manufacturer's load chart and manual. If they don't permit the move, don't make it.

response.text:
**Enclosure below the midrail (§1926.1431(e)(6))**
- The platform needs a guardrail system that meets Subpart M.
- It must be enclosed **at least from the toeboard to the midrail** with either:
  - solid construction material, or
  - expanded metal with openings **no greater than ½ inch**.
- Points where personal fall arrest systems attach must meet Subpart M anchorage requirements.

**Gates and doors (§1926.1431(e)(8))**
These rules apply to every type of access gate or door, including swinging, sliding and folding ones.
- **It must not swing outward**, with one exception. It may swing outward if the platform's size, such as a 1-person platform, makes it **infeasible** for the door to swing inward and still allow the occupant to enter safely.
- It must have **a device that prevents accidental opening**. This applies even if the outward-swing exception applies.

**Related design requirements for your build (§1926.1431(e))**
- **Designer:** A qualified person familiar with structural design must design the platform and its attachment/suspension system (e)(1).
- **Strength:** The platform must support, without failure, its own weight plus at least **5 times the maximum intended load**. This criterion excludes the guardrail system and fall arrest anchorages (e)(4).
- **Welding:** A certified welder familiar with the weld grades, types and materials in the design must do all welding (e)(5).
- **Grab rail:** One is required inside the entire perimeter, except at access gates or doors (e)(7).

This isn't the full list of platform, testing or hoisting requirements in §1926.1431. These answers are for construction work under Subpart CC.

**In construction, you wait 30 days** if the manufacturer hasn't acknowledged your request or started its review (§1926.1434(a)(2)). This applies to modifications or additions that affect the crane's capacity or safe operation (§1926.1434(a)).

To use this route, you must have given the manufacturer a **detailed description** of the modification and **asked it to approve it**. Sending plans without asking for approval doesn't meet that condition.

After 30 days, you still can't make the change until **all** of these are met (§1926.1434(a)(2)(i)–(ii)):
- A **registered professional engineer (RPE)** who is a qualified person for that equipment **approves** the modification and **specifies the equipment configurations** the approval covers.
- That RPE **modifies load charts, procedures, instruction manuals, and instruction plates/tags/decals** as necessary to match the modification.
- The equipment's **original safety factor isn't reduced**.

**If the manufacturer has responded in some way:**
- **It agreed to review but hasn't finished:** the limit is **120 days** from the date it got your detailed description. The same RPE and safety factor conditions apply (§1926.1434(a)(4)).
- **It declined to review the technical merits:** you don't have to wait out the 30 days, but the same conditions apply (§1926.1434(a)(2)).
- **It reviewed the technical safety merits and rejected the proposal, explaining why in writing:** the modification is **prohibited**. If it rejects it without that explanation, you may treat this as a refusal to review (§1926.1434(b)).

Check for an acknowledgment by any route, and keep proof of what you sent, your approval request and the date it was received.

**General industry:** these waiting periods come from the construction rule. For overhead and gantry cranes under §1910.179, see §1910.179(b)(3). It allows modification and rerating if the modifications and supporting structure are thoroughly checked for the new rated load by a qualified engineer or the equipment manufacturer. The crane must also be load tested under §1910.179(k)(2).

**It depends on which refusal you got.** This applies to construction under Subpart CC. A counterweight addition that affects capacity or safe operation is prohibited unless an exception in §1926.1434 is met.

**Written rejection with reasons: No.** If the OEM reviewed the technical safety merits, rejected the proposal and explained why in writing, the modification is prohibited (§1926.1434(b)). A registered professional engineer's (RPE's) approval doesn't override this. Check that the letter meets those conditions.

**Phone-only "no": Possibly.** If the OEM rejects the proposal without explaining its reasons in writing, you may treat that as a refusal to review under §1926.1434(a)(2) (see §1926.1434(b)). This doesn't by itself authorize the work. You need all of the following:

- **Request:** The OEM was given a detailed description of the proposed modification and asked to approve it (§1926.1434(a)(2)).
- **Engineer:** An RPE who is also a qualified person for the equipment involved must:
  - approve the modification and specify the equipment configurations the approval covers, **and**
  - modify load charts, procedures, instruction manuals and instruction plates/tags/decals as necessary to match the modification (§1926.1434(a)(2)(i)).
- **Safety factor:** The equipment's original safety factor must not be reduced (§1926.1434(a)(2)(ii)).

If the OEM later sends written reasons, or you already have them for this same proposal in another document or email, don't rely on the phone-call route without resolving that first. I'd keep a record of what you sent, when you sent it and what the OEM said.

**Before returning the crane to service:** A qualified person must inspect the modified equipment after the modification is completed and before initial use. The inspection must confirm the work was done in accordance with the §1926.1434 approval and must include functional testing (§1926.1412(a)).

**Exception:** §1926.1434 doesn't apply to modifications made or approved by the US military.

This answer doesn't cover general industry work under Part 1910, which has different provisions. It also doesn't address warranty, contract or liability issues.

**No, don't zip tie it. In construction it violates OSHA whenever §1926.1425(c) applies.** That paragraph applies when employees are **in the fall zone** and are hooking, unhooking or guiding a load, or making the initial connection of a load to a component or structure. A rigger unhooking a choker within the fall zone is covered. All of these must be met:

- The load is rigged to prevent unintentional displacement (§1926.1425(c)(1)).
- **Hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent** are used (§1926.1425(c)(2)). A latch tied open can't self-close. The exception allows "J" hooks for setting wooden trusses; it isn't permission to tie back a latch.
- A qualified rigger rigs the materials (§1926.1425(c)(3)).

**Other points**
- **Outside those conditions:** §1926.1425(c) doesn't reach every lift, but that doesn't make tying back the latch approved. I can't confirm whether the hook or rigging manufacturer allows it. Subpart H rigging rules are also outside the regulations I cover.
- **Hoisting personnel:** The rule is stricter. A hook must be a type that can be closed and locked, eliminating the throat opening. The regulation also allows an alloy anchor-type shackle with a bolt, nut and retaining pin (§1926.1431(g)).
- **General industry (1910):** §1926.1425 doesn't apply to general industry work. Don't treat that as permission. The answer there depends on the equipment and setup under §§1910.179, .180 or .184.

**What to do now:** Stop the lift setup, remove the zip tie and check that the latch closes freely and isn't damaged. Hooks and latches are also inspection items under §1926.1412. If the choker is hard to remove, have the qualified rigger fix the cause with suitable rigging or hardware while keeping a working self-closing latch or its equivalent.

**Yes, possibly. §1926.1434(a)(5) covers multiple manufacturers of equipment designed for marine work sites.** It applies to modifications or additions that affect the crane's capacity or safe operation, which are prohibited unless one of the exceptions in §1926.1434(a) is met.

**To use (a)(5), all of these must be true:**
1. The equipment is **designed for use on marine work sites**.
2. It **contains major structural components from more than one manufacturer**.
3. A **registered professional engineer (RPE) who is a qualified person for this equipment**:
   - approves the modification or addition and **specifies the equipment configurations** the approval applies to (§1926.1434(a)(2)(i)(A)), and
   - modifies the **load charts, procedures, instruction manuals and instruction plates, tags and decals** as necessary to match the change (§1926.1434(a)(2)(i)(B)).
4. The **original safety factor of the equipment is not reduced** (§1926.1434(a)(2)(ii)).

Unlike the manufacturer-refusal and 120-day exceptions in (a)(2) and (a)(4), (a)(5) does not require you to first ask a manufacturer to approve the change or to wait for a response.

**Cautions**
- **Written rejection:** The change is prohibited if the manufacturer reviews its technical safety merits, rejects it and explains why in writing (§1926.1434(b)). If you have already received such a rejection, don't assume (a)(5) gets around it. If the manufacturer rejects it without written reasons, you may treat that as a refusal to review under (a)(2) (§1926.1434(b)).
- **Marine design:** A base and boom from different companies isn't enough by itself. Being mounted on a barge also doesn't by itself show that the equipment was *designed* for marine work sites. Confirm and document this. I can't determine it from your description.
- **Military exception:** §1926.1434(a) and (b) don't apply to modifications made or approved by the US military (§1926.1434(c)).
- **Floating crane rules:** Also check §1926.1437, which has additional requirements for floating cranes and cranes on barges. Meeting §1926.1434 doesn't replace them.

**This applies to your crane:** a 2015 hydraulic truck-mounted boom crane was built after November 8, 2010, so §1926.1433's prototype testing rule for mobile cranes applies, assuming its rated capacity is over 2,000 lb. This assumes it isn't a type Subpart CC treats separately, such as an articulating (knuckle-boom) crane. I'm working from memory without the regulation text open, so check the paragraph letters and wording against the current §1926.1433.

**(1) Prototype test options (§1926.1433(c))**

The crane must meet **either** option:

- **Option A (SAE J1063, Nov. 1993, for cantilevered booms such as hydraulic booms):**
  - All tests listed in SAE J1063 Table 1 must be performed to load all critical structural elements to their respective stress limits.
  - All strength margins in SAE J1063 Table 2 must be met.
  - SAE J987 is the counterpart for pendant-supported lattice booms, so it isn't the one for your hydraulic boom.
- **Option B (BS EN 13000:2004):**
  - The crane must meet that standard's testing and verification requirements.
  - For cantilevered booms, there is an added condition: the analysis methodology (computer modeling) must demonstrate that all SAE J1063 load cases meet the strength margins in SAE J1063 Table 2.

**(2) Can computer modeling replace physical testing?**

- **Option A:** The rule says the Table 1 tests must be **performed**. As I recall it, §1926.1433 does not itself let you substitute modeling for them.
- **Option B:** Computer modeling has an explicit role, but within BS EN 13000's **testing and verification** requirements. The J1063 modeling condition is an addition to those requirements. It does not by itself waive any physical testing that EN 13000 requires.

So I find **no blanket permission to replace physical testing with modeling**. I can't tell you from these regulations which specific tests EN 13000 requires physically, or what substitutions the text of EN 13000 or SAE J1063 may allow. For that, check those standards. To find out how your crane was qualified, ask the manufacturer which option it used and for its supporting documentation.

**No.** A spotter or any other workaround can't substitute for a working trolley brake on a tower crane in construction.

- **Required device:** A trolley brake is a required safety device. It must set automatically if there is a pressure loss or power failure (§1926.1435(d)(2)(vii)).
- **Before operating:** Operations must not begin unless the required safety devices are in proper working order (§1926.1435(d)(3)).
- **If it fails during operation:** The operator must **safely stop operations**. They must not resume until the brake works properly again, and **alternative measures are not permitted** (§1926.1435(d)(3)).

**Don't confuse this with operational aids.** Tower crane operational aids, such as trolley travel limiting devices, are covered separately in §1926.1435(e). That paragraph allows specified temporary alternative measures, subject to its conditions and repair deadlines. Those allowances don't apply to the trolley brake.

**What to do now:** Stop safely and keep the crane out of that operation until the brake is repaired and working properly. This answer doesn't cover how to secure the trolley or load, or how to troubleshoot or repair the brake. For those, follow the manufacturer's procedures, which I can't supply from these regulations.

**Load test after erecting a tower crane (§1926.1435(f)(2), post-erection inspection)**

This applies in addition to the post-assembly inspection requirements of §1926.1412(c).

- **When:** A load test must be conducted **after each erection**.
- **Test weights:** Use either **certified weights** or **weights scaled on a certified scale with a current certificate of calibration**.

**There is a legal temporary measure, but you can't just keep running.** On a tower crane, the trolley travel limiting device is a **Category I operational aid** (§1926.1435(e)).

**Before you continue:** If it failed during operations, **safely stop** until a temporary alternative measure is in place or the device is repaired. If it was already out, don't start without that measure (§1926.1435(e)).

**Temporary alternative measures (use at least one)** (§1926.1435(e), Category I, trolley travel limiting device):
- **Mark the trolley rope** where the operator can see it, at a point that gives enough time to stop the trolley before it reaches the end stops, **or**
- **Use a spotter** when operating **within 10 feet of the outer or inner trolley end stops**.

**Conditions**
- **Manufacturer:** If it specifies more protective alternative measures, follow those (§1926.1435(e)). I don't have your crane's procedures, so check them.
- **Repair deadline:** Repair it **within 7 calendar days** after the deficiency occurs. The exception is when the employer documents that it ordered the necessary parts within those 7 days. The repair must then be completed **within 7 calendar days of receiving the parts** (§1926.1435(e), Category I).
- **End stops:** Trolley end stops are required at **both ends** of trolley travel and are a **safety device**, not an operational aid. If one is missing or not working properly, stop. No temporary alternative is allowed, and work can't resume until it's fixed (§1926.1435(d)). The rope mark or spotter doesn't replace the stops.

**Don't treat the end stops as your limit.** The purpose of the limiting device is to keep the trolley from running into them. These measures also don't authorize jumpering or altering the switch circuit.

**Now:** Report the failure to your supervisor and record when it occurred, since that starts the 7-day period.

**Six weeks is over the 30-day threshold.** For a derrick taken out of service for **30 days or more**, secure the boom by one of these methods (§1926.1436, "Securing the boom"; I believe this is paragraph (p), but check the letter against the current text):

- **Lay it down.**
- **Secure it to a stationary member**, as nearly under the boom head as possible, by attaching a sling to the load block.
- **Guy derricks:** lift the boom to a vertical position and secure it to the mast.
- **Stiffleg derricks:** secure the boom against the stiffleg.

Also, whenever the boom is held in a fixed position, **dogs, pawls or other positive holding mechanisms on the boom hoist must be engaged** (same provision).

**Before returning it to service:** equipment idle for **3 months or more** needs a qualified person to inspect it under the monthly inspection requirements (§1926.1412(h)). Six weeks doesn't reach that trigger, but other inspections that apply, such as the shift inspection (§1926.1412(d)), still do.

This is the construction rule. I can't tell you the manufacturer's lay-down or securing procedure from these regulations, so get that separately for your derrick.

response.text:
**Test load: §1926.1436(n)(3)**

Before first use, a **competent person** must load test the reinstalled derrick.
- The test load must be **at least 100% and no more than 110% of rated capacity**, unless the manufacturer or a qualified person recommends otherwise.
- In **no event** may it be less than the **maximum anticipated load**.

The test must include:
- Hoisting the load a few inches and holding it, to verify that the derrick supports it and the hoist brake(s) hold it
- Swinging through the full range, if applicable, at the maximum allowable working radius for the test load
- Booming up and down within the allowable working radius for the test load
- Lowering, stopping and holding the load with the brake(s)

You may not use the derrick unless the competent person determines it **passed**.

**If your biggest pick is heavier**
- **Heavier than your planned test load:** increase the test load to at least the weight of that pick.
- **Heavier than rated capacity at the planned configuration and radius:** a bigger test load **does not raise the rated capacity or authorize the pick**. The derrick must not be operated above rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)(1), applied to derricks through §1926.1436(b)). Don't just test to the heavier weight. Change the lift plan or configuration so the pick is within the rating. Any change to the derrick's capacity is a separate matter that this load test doesn't settle.

**Also required before first use: §1926.1436(n)(1)–(2)**
- **Anchorages:** A qualified person must approve them, including the supporting structure if applicable. For rock or hairpin anchorages, the qualified person must decide whether special testing is needed, and any required testing must be done.
- **No-load functional test:** A competent person must run the hook(s) and boom through their full travel and swing fully in each direction. The test also includes actuating the anti two-block, boom hoist limit, locking, limiting and indicating devices, where provided.

**Paperwork: §1926.1436(n)(4)–(5)**
- **What to record:** Document the tests with the **date, test results and name of the tester**.
- **How long to keep it:** Keep it until the derrick is **retested or dismantled, whichever comes first**.
- **Who can see it:** During that period, it must be available to **all persons who conduct inspections under Subpart CC**.

These are the federal construction rules. They don't cover manufacturer test procedures or any additional state-plan requirements.

**For your crane, the OSHA maximum is 7° of list and 7° of trim** (§1926.1437(m)(2), Table M1). This is the row for equipment designed for marine use and permanently attached, other than derricks, with a rated capacity over 25 tons. The 25-tons-or-less row is 5°. **I can't give you one fixed barge list/trim number for a land crane on a deck barge.** As I understand §1926.1437, the limit depends on your crane, barge and conditions. I'm working from memory without the rule text, so check the paragraph letters and wording before relying on this.

- **Which rules apply:** A crawler placed on a barge falls under the land crane provisions of **§1926.1437(n)**, not the provisions for floating cranes designed for marine use in §1926.1437(m). Don't borrow the list/trim table for floating cranes or derricks and apply it to your crawler.
- **Capacity:** The rated capacity must be reduced as needed for the effects of **list, trim, wave action and wind** (§1926.1437(n)). A land load chart can't be assumed to apply on the barge.
- **3° figure:** It doesn't automatically make 3° your allowable barge list or trim, or establish what capacity you have at 3°. Confirm in writing:
  - the capacity chart and configuration that go with it
  - whether it applies to side slope, fore-and-aft slope or both combined, in every swing position
  - whether it covers dynamic motion or only a static out-of-level condition
- **What sets the barge limit:** It has to keep the crane within the manufacturer's limits and keep the barge stable under the planned loads, radii and swing positions. Account for list and trim together, initial barge attitude, ballast, deck load movement, deck or mat deflection, and wave motion. If the barge analysis gives a lower limit than 3°, use the lower one.
- **Who determines it:** Check §1926.1437(n) for the roles of the manufacturer and a qualified person in modifying capacity and evaluating the barge. Have the lift-specific limits documented before work starts.
- **Related items:** Also review §1926.1437(n) for the requirements on physically securing the crane against shifting and on the barge's condition, and the rest of §1926.1437 for any other provisions that apply.

I can't calculate your barge's list or trim, or the derated capacity, from these regulations. That takes the manufacturer's data, the barge stability information and a qualified person's analysis. Any contract, Coast Guard or other standard requirements are also outside what I can answer here.

**It depends mostly on what's still on the hook and whether anyone is riding it.** The diving rules (such as 29 CFR 1910 Subpart T) are outside the regulations I answer from. I can't tell you what they or your dive plan require, so check with the dive supervisor before making any other pick.

**Other picks while the divers are down**
- **Platform on one line, divers suspended on it:** My understanding is that §1926.1431 bars lifts on any of the crane's other load lines while personnel are suspended on a platform. I'm not certain of the paragraph number, so check the text.
- **Divers off the crane and in the water:** I can't confirm from these regulations that other picks are allowed, or that a particular Subpart CC provision bans them. Don't treat that as permission. Swing, loads over the dive area, barge list or trim, and fouling the divers' umbilicals all need to be cleared with the dive supervisor.
- **Using the crane to lower them at all:** This is hoisting personnel. Under §1926.1431(a), it's prohibited unless the employer shows that conventional means would be more hazardous or aren't possible because of the worksite's structural design or conditions. Other §1926.1431 requirements can also apply. For a crane on a barge, check §1926.1437 too.

**Does the operator have to stay at the controls?**
- **Platform occupied:** Plan on yes. My understanding is that §1926.1431 requires the operator to stay at the controls while the engine is running and the platform is occupied. Check the exact paragraph and wording. Don't use the suspended-load exception below to leave while divers are on the hook.
- **Any suspended load:** The general rule in §1926.1417(e)(1) is that the operator must not leave the controls.
- **Exception, §1926.1417(e)(2):** The operator may leave the controls only if all of these are met:
  - The operator stays next to the equipment and does no other duties.
  - The load will be held longer than in normal lifting operations.
  - A competent person determines it's safe and puts in place the measures needed to restrain the boom hoist and telescoping, load, swing, and outrigger or stabilizer functions.
  - Barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone.
- **Nothing suspended and nobody on the hook:** §1926.1417(e)(1) doesn't require the operator to stay just because divers are in the water. The dive rules or your dive plan might.

**To pin this down:** Are the divers riding a stage or platform, and does it stay on the hook, occupied or empty, while they're down?

**It depends mainly on the boom type.**

**Lattice boom: Subpart CC's anti two-block requirement doesn't apply** to marine operations that don't hoist personnel. Pile driving work is also excepted (§1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)(C)). So setting sheet pile from a floating lattice boom crane with nobody hoisted falls within the marine exception.

**Telescopic boom made after February 28, 1992: yes, you need it.** It must automatically prevent damage from two-blocking at all points where it could occur (§1926.1416(d)(3)(i)). The lattice boom exception doesn't cover telescopic booms.

If a required device isn't working properly:
- **Temporary measures:** Either clearly mark the cable, where the operator can easily see it, at a point that gives enough time to stop the hoist, **or** use a spotter when extending the boom (§1926.1416(d)(3)(i)).
- **Repair deadline:** It's a Category I aid, so it must be repaired within **7 calendar days** after the deficiency occurs. If you document that you ordered the parts within those 7 days, the repair must be done within 7 calendar days of receiving them (§1926.1416(d)).

**Before you rely on the exception:**
- **Hoisting people:** If the crane will hoist personnel, the exception no longer covers that work, and the personnel hoisting rules in §1926.1431 apply.
- **Other floating crane rules:** The exception only covers this anti two-block requirement. The floating crane rules in §1926.1437 and other applicable Subpart CC requirements still apply.
- **Derricks and older cranes:** If your rig is a derrick, or a telescopic crane made on or before February 28, 1992, check it separately. Derricks also have their own section, §1926.1436.
- **Other requirements:** I can't tell from these regulations whether the manufacturer, your contract or company policy requires the device anyway.

**What boom type is on your crane?**

**Certification: no, OSHA's Subpart CC doesn't require it for sideboom operators.** §1926.1440(a) excludes sidebooms from §1926.1427 (operator training, certification and evaluation). OSHA also doesn't require NCCCO specifically for other cranes. §1926.1427 sets out certification/licensing routes without requiring one organization.

**You still have to train them.** The employer must train operators excepted from §1926.1427 on the safe operation of the equipment they'll use (§1926.1430(c)(2)).

**Live boom: it depends on the manufacture date and the job.** Under §1926.1440(b), live boom sidebooms are prohibited if manufactured **after November 8, 2010**. An older one isn't banned by that date rule, but §1926.1426 still applies, except paragraph (a)(2)(i).

Under §1926.1426(a)(1), live boom equipment can't be used when:
- an employee is in the fall zone of the boom or load
- an employee is being hoisted
- the load or boom is directly over a power line, or within the area extending the §1926.1408 Table A clearance distance to either side of it
- the load is over a shaft (subject to the exception in that paragraph)
- the load is over a cofferdam, with an exception where no employees are in the fall zone
- lifting is being done in a refinery or tank farm

**Other sideboom rules:** §1926.1440(a) also excludes §1926.1402 (ground conditions), §1926.1415 (safety devices) and §1926.1416 (operational aids). The rest of Subpart CC applies as modified by §1926.1440, which has additional sideboom provisions, so check the full section. These exclusions don't remove requirements found elsewhere.

Under **§1926.1441(d)(2)**, covered equipment manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 must have **either**:
- an anti two-block device that meets **§1926.1416(d)(3)**, **or**

- **Original equipment:** If it came with an anti two-block device or other safety devices or operational aids, they must be maintained according to the manufacturer's procedures (**§1926.1441(d)(1)**).

**General personnel-hoisting rule, §1926.1431(a):** Using equipment to hoist employees is prohibited unless you can show that conventional access (ladder, stairway, aerial lift, personnel hoist, scaffold, etc.) would be **more hazardous or isn't possible** because of the structure's design or worksite conditions. - **Safety devices:** Requirements cover items such as anti-two-block protection and control of load line and boom movement (§1926.1431(d)).
- **Before lifting people:** You need a trial lift, proof testing, inspection and a pre-lift meeting (§1926.1431(h), (m)).
- **During the lift:** Work-practice and fall protection requirements also apply (§1926.1431).

This isn't the full list.

**Manufacturer limits:** Check the manual for any restriction on lifting people. I can't tell you what your model allows from these regulations.

**For now, don't lift him.** Use a ladder, stairs or a properly selected aerial lift. If this isn't construction work, such as routine maintenance under general industry rules, §1926.1431 may not be the governing rule, so tell me what the job is.

**Yes, it can be allowed** if your crane qualifies as a mobile auxiliary crane used **on the deck of a floating crane/derrick**. The exception in **§1926.1437(n)(6)** relieves you of the (n)(5) options: physical attachment, corralling, rails or a centerline cable system. It applies only if you **demonstrate that you've implemented** a plan and procedures meeting all of the following.

**What you need**
- **Engineer's plan:** A marine engineer, or a registered professional engineer familiar with floating crane/derrick design, must develop **and sign** a written plan for using the auxiliary crane. (§1926.1437(n)(6)(i))
- **Compliance without restraint:** The plan must be designed so the applicable requirements of §1926.1437 are met despite the crane's position, travel, operation and lack of attachment, corralling, rails or cable system. (n)(6)(ii)
- **Areas and limits:** It must specify where on deck the crane may be positioned, travel and operate, and the parameters and limits on that movement and operation. (n)(6)(iii)
- **Deck markings:** The permitted positioning, travel and operating areas must be marked on the deck. (n)(6)(iv)
- **Conditions:** The plan must specify the dynamic and environmental conditions that must be present to use it. (n)(6)(v)

**If the seas exceed the plan's conditions**

The crane **must be physically attached or corralled** under **Option (1), physical attachment; Option (2), corralling; or Option (4), centerline cable system**, in (n)(5). **Option (3), rails, is not listed as a fallback.** (§1926.1437(n)(6)(vi))

The system you use must also meet the (n)(5) requirements that apply to all the options, including its design by a qualified professional as specified there. In practice, I recommend having that system designed and ready on board before you rely on the plan. I also suggest setting a clear trigger, with someone assigned to monitor conditions, so the crane is secured before the limits are exceeded.

**Other requirements:** This exception covers only the (n)(5) restraint options. It doesn't waive the other applicable requirements of §1926.1437, including those for land cranes on vessels in paragraph (n), such as rated capacity and list/trim limits.

These regulations don't supply the sea-state, list or wind limits for your barge and crane, or the design of the restraint system. Those have to come from the engineering plan and design, and I can't determine them from the regulations. Manufacturer limitations also need to be checked against the manufacturer's documents.

**Where the disconnect goes (floor-operated crane)**

An **enclosed-type** switch or circuit breaker **that can be locked open** must be in the **leads from the runway conductors**. It must be **mounted on the bridge or footwalk, near the runway collectors** (§1910.179(g)(5)(iii)).

**How the operator can cut power from the floor**

You must provide **one of these** (§1910.179(g)(5)(iii)(a)–(c)):

- **(a)** A **nonconductive rope** attached to the main disconnect switch.
- **(b)** An **undervoltage trip** for the main circuit breaker, operated by an **emergency stop button in the pendant station**.
- **(c)** A **main line contactor**, operated by a **switch or pushbutton in the pendant station**.

**A separate requirement for the runway supply**

The power supply **to the runway conductors** needs its own switch or circuit breaker. It must be **on a fixed structure, accessible from the floor, and arranged to be locked open** (§1910.179(g)(5)(i)). The bridge-mounted disconnect and its floor-operated means don't replace it.

This answer applies the general industry rule for overhead and gantry cranes, §1910.179.

**This assumes bay 3 has an overhead or gantry crane covered by §1910.179.**

## Idle about 3 months
The rule for a crane idle **1 month or more but less than 6 months** is §1910.179(j)(4)(i). Before returning it to service, it needs both of these:

**1. A frequent inspection, §1910.179(j)(2),** including:
- Functional operating mechanisms, for maladjustment that interferes with proper operation
- Deterioration or leakage in lines, tanks, valves, drain pumps and other parts of air or hydraulic systems
- Hooks, for deformation or cracks
- Hoist chains, including end connections, for excessive wear, twist, distorted links that interfere with proper function, or stretch beyond the manufacturer's recommendations
- The other items in (j)(2), including functional operating mechanisms for excessive wear

For hooks and hoist chains, check the certification record requirements in (j)(2). Records include the inspection date, the inspector's signature and an identifier for the hook or chain.

**2. An idle rope inspection, §1910.179(m)(2):**
- Thoroughly inspect the rope for **all types of deterioration**.
- An **appointed or authorized person** must do it, and that person's approval is required for further use of the rope.
- A **certification record** must be available, with the inspection date, the inspector's signature and an identifier for the rope.

## Idle 8 months
For a crane idle **over 6 months**, §1910.179(j)(4)(ii) requires a **complete inspection** before service. This covers (j)(2) and (m)(2) above, **plus the periodic inspection in (j)(3)**. That includes the (j)(2) items and checks for:
- Deformed, cracked or corroded members
- Loose bolts or rivets
- Cracked or worn sheaves and drums
- Worn, cracked or distorted parts such as pins, bearings, shafts, gears, rollers, and locking and clamping devices
- Excessive wear on brake system parts, linings, pawls and ratchets
- Significant inaccuracies in load, wind and other indicators
- Gasoline, diesel, electric or other powerplants, for improper performance or noncompliance
- Excessive wear of chain drive sprockets and excessive chain stretch
- Electrical apparatus, such as pitted or deteriorated controller contactors, limit switches and pushbutton stations

## Also check
- **Exactly 6 months:** the text says "less than 6 months" and "over 6 months," so it doesn't expressly address exactly 6.
- **Standby cranes:** these have a separate rule, at least semiannual inspection under (j)(2) and (m)(2) (§1910.179(j)(4)(iii)).
- **Operator checks:** the shift checks still apply, including those for upper limit switches and hoist brakes (§1910.179(n)(4)).
- **Other equipment or work:** a mobile, crawler or truck crane in general industry falls under §1910.180. Construction work falls under Subpart CC, where different idle-equipment rules can apply. For permanently installed overhead and gantry cranes used in construction, see §1926.1438(b). If either case fits, tell me the crane type and the work.

| Crane and rules | Who inspects or approves | What's required before use |
|---|---|---|

A **written, dated report** of the rope's condition must be available for inspection. |

**For construction:**
- **Shift inspection:** A competent person must begin a visual rope inspection before each shift the equipment is used (§1926.1413(a)(1)).
- **Monthly inspection:** If it's due, the rope can't be used until the inspection shows that no corrective action under §1926.1413(a)(4) is required (§1926.1413(b)). It must be documented (§§1926.1413(b)(4), 1926.1412(e)(3)).

- **Idle equipment:** The rule for equipment idle **3 months or more** calls for a qualified person to inspect it, following the monthly inspection requirements, before use (§1926.1412(h)). Six weeks doesn't reach that threshold.

These answers assume general industry use under **29 CFR 1910.179**.

**Load test: §1910.179(k)(2)**
- The test load must **not exceed 125% of rated load, unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise.** For example, on a 10-ton rating the limit is 12.5 tons.
- This is a ceiling. The paragraph doesn't require you to test at 125%.
- Test reports must be filed where appointed personnel can readily get them.

**Upper (hoist) limit switch: §1910.179(k)(1)(ii)**
- Determine the trip setting by testing with an **empty hook**, traveling at **increasing speeds up to maximum speed**.
- Locate the actuating mechanism so it trips the switch **under all conditions** in time to **prevent the hook or hook block from contacting any part of the trolley**.
- The regulation gives no set clearance distance. For the adjustment procedure, use the manufacturer's instructions, which I don't have.

**Other checks after the rebuild**
- **If the rebuild altered the crane:** before initial use, test it for compliance with the section, including hoisting and lowering, trolley travel, bridge travel, and limit switches, locking and safety devices (§1910.179(k)(1)(i)). Altered cranes also need an initial inspection (§1910.179(j)(1)(i)). Your description alone doesn't tell me whether this rebuild counts as an alteration. For "extensively repaired" cranes, check the current wording of (k) and (j) and have your qualified or appointed person make the call.
- **If it was modified and rerated:** a qualified engineer or the manufacturer must thoroughly check the modifications and supporting structure for the new rating. The crane must be tested under (k)(2), and the new rated load must be displayed (§1910.179(b)(3)).
- **Each shift:** try out each hoist's upper limit switch with **no load**. Inch the block into the limit or run it in at slow speed. If the switch doesn't operate properly, notify the appointed person immediately (§1910.179(n)(4)(i)).
- **In normal operation:** don't use the limit switch as an operating control (§1910.179(n)(4)(ii)). The slow-speed shift check doesn't replace the increasing-speed test used to set the trip point.

If the crane is used in **construction**, also check §1926.1438, which covers overhead and gantry cranes.
