**Before you start, meet all of §1910.179(l)(2)(i):**

1. **Move the crane** to where it will interfere least with other cranes and operations in the area (§1910.179(l)(2)(i)(*a*)).
2. **Put all controllers in the off position** (§1910.179(l)(2)(i)(*b*)).
3. **Open the main or emergency switch and lock it open** (§1910.179(l)(2)(i)(*c*)).
4. **Post warning or "out of order" signs** on the crane, and also on the floor beneath it or on the hook where visible from the floor (§1910.179(l)(2)(i)(*d*)).
5. **Protect your crane from the other one.** Because the other crane is operating on the same runway, provide rail stops or other suitable means to prevent it from interfering with the idle crane (§1910.179(l)(2)(i)(*e*)). Have these in place before work begins. Signs or locking out your own crane don't physically stop the other one.

**Who can do the work:** Only designated personnel may make adjustments and repairs (§1910.179(l)(3)(i)). Brakes must be adjusted as needed to keep them functioning correctly (§1910.179(l)(3)(ii)).

**Before returning it to service:** Don't operate the crane until guards are reinstalled, safety devices reactivated and maintenance equipment removed (§1910.179(l)(2)(ii)). Check the brake requirements in §1910.179(f) for the brake you worked on.

**Not covered here:**
- **Other energy and hazards:** General lockout/tagout (§1910.147) and fall protection rules are outside the regulations I answer from. Check them and your site's procedures, including how to control stored energy or runway power that stays live after you open the crane's switch.
- **Brake procedure:** For disassembly, adjustment settings and wear limits specific to your brake, use the manufacturer's instructions. I can't give those from these regulations. Before releasing a hoist brake, make sure you have the manufacturer's method for securing the load block and drum.

This assumes general industry work. If it's construction work, check §1926.1438 for which overhead crane requirements apply.

response.text:
The distance depends on your specific crane (drum capacity, rope length and diameter, boom length and angle, and parts of line), so I can't give you a depth from these regulations. What they do set is the minimum rope that has to stay on the drum.

- **Construction (Subpart CC):** The drum must never have less than **2 full wraps** of wire rope remaining, in any operating position or during operation (§1926.1417(s)(1)). Also, neither the load nor the boom may be lowered below the point where **less than 2 full wraps** remain on their drums (§1926.1417(s)(2)). So stop while 2 full wraps are still on, not when the drum is empty.
- **General industry overhead and gantry cranes:** With the load block on the floor, at least **2 wraps** must remain on each hoisting drum, unless a lower-limit device is provided (§1910.179(h)(2)(iii)(a)).
- **General industry crawler, locomotive and truck cranes:** At least **2 full wraps** must remain on the drum at all times (§1910.180(h)(3)(ii)(a)).

These are regulatory minimums. The manufacturer may require more wraps, and its requirement may matter under the manufacturer-procedure rules, but I don't have your crane's manual.

**For your actual maximum hook depth,** check the manufacturer's rope and reeving data or load chart notes, and confirm the length of the rope actually installed, since a replacement or shortened rope changes the answer. More parts of line use up more rope for each foot of hook travel. Allow for any travel below grade, and don't count on the last 2 wraps.

If you tell me which type of crane you're running and whether it's construction or general industry work, I can point you to the rule that applies.

**If you're running an overhead or gantry crane covered by §1910.179, yes, you have to check it, and no, you can't use it to stop the hoist.**

- **Shift check (§1910.179(n)(4)(i)):** At the beginning of each operator's shift, try out the upper limit switch of **each hoist** with **no load**. Use extreme care: **inch** the block into the limit or run it in at **slow speed**. If the switch doesn't operate properly, **immediately notify the appointed person**.
- **Every pick (§1910.179(n)(4)(ii)):** The hoist limit switch that controls the upper travel of the load block must **never be used as an operating control**. Stop the hoist with your normal controls before the block reaches the limit.

**Other cranes:** This answer doesn't carry over to mobile or other construction cranes. In construction, anti two-block and other upper-limit devices depend on the crane type and, in some cases, its manufacture date (see §1926.1416, and §1926.1412(d) for shift inspections). For permanently installed overhead and gantry cranes used in construction, §1926.1438(b) points to many of the §1910.179 requirements.

If you're on something other than an overhead or gantry crane, tell me the crane type and whether the work is construction or general industry.

**Not as a routine practice.** Under §1910.179(n)(3)(iv), overhead and gantry cranes **must not be used for side pulls unless a responsible person specifically authorizes it** after determining that:

- the crane's **stability** won't be endangered, **and**
- **no parts of the crane will be overstressed.**

If you don't have that authorization and determination for this pull, don't do it. Being the operator, or having a light skid, doesn't by itself meet the condition.

**For a normal lift,** bring the hook over the load so it won't swing before you hoist (§1910.179(n)(3)(ii)(c)). The load must also be well secured and balanced in the sling or lifting device before it's lifted more than a few inches (§1910.179(n)(3)(i)).

**On a construction job:** §1926.1438 governs overhead and gantry cranes, and which rules apply depends on whether the crane is permanently installed. For a **permanently installed** one, §1926.1438(b) applies §1910.179 requirements, with exceptions that don't remove the side-pull rule. If yours **isn't permanently installed**, check §1926.1438(c) before relying on the exception above, because different requirements apply.

These regulations can't tell me whether your crane can safely take this pull. That may require the manufacturer's information or an evaluation of the crane.

**Yes. In construction, the trigger is 90% or more of maximum *line pull*** (§1926.1417(s)):

- **Test:** Lift the load a few inches and apply the brakes.
- **When:** Do this each time you handle a load at or above that threshold.
- **Repetitive and duty cycle lifts:** If each lift is 90% or more of maximum line pull, the test applies to the first lift but not the successive ones.

**Line pull isn't the same as the crane's rated capacity.** A load near the load chart limit isn't necessarily at 90% of maximum line pull, and the reverse is also true. Check the line pull for your hoist and setup. I can't determine that value from these regulations. You also must not exceed rated capacity, and you have to verify the load's weight as §1926.1417(o) requires.

**If your work falls under general industry**, the trigger is a load **approaching the rated load**, with no percentage given. Raise it a few inches and apply the brakes:

- **Overhead and gantry cranes:** §1910.179(n)(3)(vii)
- **Crawler, locomotive and truck cranes:** §1910.180(h)(3)(vii)

**Under 29 CFR 1910.180(c)(1)(i) (general industry), load ratings for crawler cranes must not exceed these percentages of tipping load:**

| Crawler crane configuration | Maximum rating (% of tipping load) |
|---|---|
| Without outriggers | **75%** |
| Using outriggers, fully extended | **85%** |

- **Basis:** The tipping load is the load that produces tipping or balance with the boom in the **least stable direction** relative to the mounting, at the stated boom length and working radius. The percentages are subject to the conditions in §1910.180(c)(1).
- **Not just stability:** These are stability limits. A rating may be limited by something other than tipping, such as structural strength, so don't calculate a capacity from these percentages. Use the crane's load rating chart.
- **Construction work:** These figures come from the general industry rule. For construction, check the design requirements in §1926.1433, which depend partly on manufacture date and refer to outside consensus standards. Don't assume the 75%/85% values apply to a particular construction crane. In operation, you must not exceed the rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)).

**Yes, the rope needs sign-off.** For a crane idle about 3 months, do both of the following before returning it to service.

## 1. Crane: frequent inspection
A crane idle **1 month or more but less than 6 months** needs an inspection meeting §1910.180(d)(3) and (g)(2)(ii) (**§1910.180(d)(5)(i)**).

The (d)(3) items include:
- Control mechanisms, for maladjustment, excessive wear and contamination
- Safety devices, for malfunction
- Air and hydraulic systems, for deterioration or leakage
- Hooks, for deformation or cracks, including throat opening more than **15%** over normal or twist of more than **10°** from the plane of the unbent hook
- Rope reeving, for noncompliance with the manufacturer's recommendations
- Electrical apparatus, for malfunction, excessive deterioration, dirt and moisture

The list isn't exhaustive. Carefully examine any deficiency and determine whether it is a safety hazard (§1910.180(d)(3)).

## 2. Rope: thorough idle-rope inspection (§1910.180(g)(2)(ii))
This applies to **all rope** idle a month or more because the crane it's installed on was shut down or stored.
- **When:** before the rope is used.
- **Scope:** all types of deterioration. For what to look for, see §1910.180(g)(1), such as diameter reduction, broken or worn wires, corrosion, damaged or improperly applied end connections, kinking, crushing, cutting and unstranding.
- **Who:** an **appointed or authorized person**.
- **Sign-off:** **that person's approval is required** for further use of the rope.
- **Record:** a certification record with the **inspection date, the inspector's signature and an identifier for the rope** must be available for inspection.

## Other points
- **Other records:** check §1910.180(d)(6) for certification records on critical items. Overdue periodic or monthly items should also be brought current before use; that is my practical advice, as (d)(5)(i) itself specifies only (d)(3) and (g)(2)(ii).
- **Longer idle time:** if the crane has been idle **over 6 months**, it needs the (d)(3) **and** periodic (d)(4) inspections, plus the (g)(2)(ii) rope inspection (§1910.180(d)(5)(ii)). Confirm the date it was last in service.
- **Standby cranes:** if this is a standby crane, it must be inspected at least **semiannually** under (d)(3) and (g)(2)(ii) (§1910.180(d)(5)(iii)).
- **Changes during the layup:** if the crane was altered, other requirements apply, including initial inspection (§1910.180(d)(1)) and testing (§1910.180(e)).

Manufacturer requirements for returning your model to service are outside what I can answer from these regulations.

**It depends on whether the work falls under construction or general industry, and on the type of crane.** A boom suggests a mobile or locomotive crane.

**General industry: crawler, locomotive and truck cranes (§1910.180)**
- **Maximum test load:** no more than **110% of the rated load at any selected working radius** (§1910.180(e)(2)). This is a ceiling, not a required test weight.
- **Paperwork:** **written reports must be available showing the test procedures and confirming the adequacy of the repairs or alterations** (§1910.180(e)(2)).
- **Rerating:** if the crane needs to be rerated, additional test requirements apply. It can't be rated above its original load ratings unless the crane manufacturer or final assembler approves (§1910.180(e)(2)).

**Construction (Subpart CC)**
- **Inspection:** a repair to load-sustaining structural components requires a **qualified person's inspection after the repair and before initial use**. It must include functional testing of the repaired parts and other components the repair may have affected (§1926.1412(b)).
- **Acceptance criteria:** the qualified person checks the repair against the manufacturer's criteria, where applicable and available. If they aren't, the qualified person determines whether a registered professional engineer (RPE) is needed to develop criteria. If an RPE isn't needed, the employer must ensure a qualified person develops them. The crane can't be used until the inspection shows the criteria are met (§1926.1412(b)).
- **Test weight and paperwork:** §1926.1412(b) doesn't set a general post-repair load-test percentage or require a written report for this inspection. This doesn't clear you to exceed the load chart. Manufacturer requirements also matter, and I can't determine your crane's test procedure from these regulations.
- **Modifications and derricks:** if the work changed the original design or affects capacity, also check §1926.1434, which covers equipment modifications and has its own approval conditions. Derricks have separate provisions in §1926.1436.

**If it's actually an overhead or gantry crane in general industry:** the test load can't exceed **125% of rated load unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise**. Test reports must be **on file and readily available to appointed personnel** (§1910.179(k)(2)).

**It depends on whether the job falls under general industry or construction.**

**General industry (crawler, locomotive and truck cranes covered by §1910.180):** If the load is limited by structural competence rather than stability, you must ascertain that its weight **has been determined within ±10% before you lift it** (§1910.180(h)(1)(ii)). You also can't exceed the rated load, except for permitted testing (§1910.180(h)(1)(i)). The 10% is about how accurately you know the weight. It doesn't allow you to go 10% over the chart.

**Construction (Subpart CC):** §1926.1417(o) states **no ± tolerance** and makes no separate weight rule for structural versus stability limits. You can't exceed rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)(1)), and you must verify the load is within it by **at least one** of these methods (§1926.1417(o)(3)):

- **Determine the weight first, (o)(3)(i):** Use an industry-recognized source (such as the load's manufacturer), an industry-recognized calculation method, or other equally reliable means. If you ask for this information, it must be given to you before the lift.
- **Check it as you begin hoisting, (o)(3)(ii):** Use a load weighing device, load moment indicator, rated capacity indicator or rated capacity limiter to determine whether the load exceeds **75% of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius you'll use during the lift**. If it does, don't proceed until you've verified the weight under (o)(3)(i).

In construction, don't treat ±10% from §1910.180 as extra capacity or as a substitute for these steps. If the possible error in your weight could put the load over the chart, you haven't shown it's within rated capacity. Count rigging and other deductions as your crane's load chart directs; I can't tell you those from these regulations.

**§1910.180 gives no clearance distance of its own.** As I understand §1910.180(j), "Operations near overhead lines," it refers you to **§1910.333(c)(3)**. That section is outside the regulations I answer from, so I can't give you its distances or conditions. Ask your safety or electrical lead which rules cover the job, including any other electrical standard for your type of plant.

**If the job is construction work,** Subpart CC applies, even at a plant. The main requirements are:

- **Work zone (§1926.1408(a)(1)):** Identify it by marking boundaries and prohibiting operation past them, or treat it as 360° around the crane, up to maximum working radius.
- **20 ft check (§1926.1408(a)(2)):** If any part of the equipment, load line or load could get closer than 20 ft, choose one:
  - **Option 1:** Have the utility confirm the line is de-energized, and visibly ground it at the worksite.
  - **Option 2:** Keep at least 20 ft clearance.
  - **Option 3:** Get the voltage from the utility and use Table A.
- **Encroachment precautions (§1926.1408(b)):** These apply under Options 2 and 3. They include a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if tag lines are used, and an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs. You also need at least one additional listed measure, such as a proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, range control warning device, range limiting device or insulating link. Check (b) for the conditions on each.

**Table A minimum clearances (§1926.1408):**

| Voltage (kV, AC) | Minimum distance |
|---|---|
| Up to 50 | 10 ft |
| Over 50 to 200 | 15 ft |
| Over 200 to 350 | 20 ft |
| Over 350 to 500 | 25 ft |
| Over 500 to 750 | 35 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 | 45 ft |
| Over 1,000 | Set by the utility/owner-operator or a qualified registered professional engineer |

- **Over 350 kV (§1926.1409):** The 20 ft trigger distance becomes 50 ft. Over 1,000 kV, the utility/owner-operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the distance.
- **Traveling under or near lines with no load:** See §1926.1411 and Table T. Its distances differ from Table A.
- **Working under lines:** See §1926.1408(d) for the restrictions and exceptions.

**Don't make any picks, even small ones, unless the manufacturer's load chart covers the crane's exact current configuration, including no counterweight.** The full-counterweight chart no longer applies, and you can't safely estimate or derate from it. A light load at a long radius can still be too much.

**General industry (plant maintenance or production work), truck cranes**
- You can't load the crane beyond its rated load, except for permitted testing: §1910.180(h)(3)(i). The rating has to match the crane as it's configured.
- A durable load rating chart must be fixed in the cab, visible to the operator at the controls: §1910.180(c)(2).
- Altered cranes must be inspected before initial use: §1910.180(d)(1). I can't say from the text alone that every counterweight removal counts as an "alteration."

**Construction work**
- You must follow the manufacturer's procedures that apply to operating the equipment: §1926.1417(a).
- Load charts and operating procedures must be readily available in the cab: §1926.1417(c).
- You can't exceed rated capacity: §1926.1417(o).
- After assembly, a qualified person must inspect the equipment before use to confirm it's configured according to the manufacturer's criteria: §1926.1412(c). This matters when the counterweight goes back on. Reinstalling it is also subject to the assembly rules in §§1926.1403–1926.1406.

**What to do now**
1. Keep the crane out of lifting service and tell your supervisor and operators.
2. Check the load chart and manual for a zero-counterweight configuration. Match the counterweight, boom length and any jib, radius or angle, outrigger or tire setup, and working quadrant, plus all chart notes.
3. If it's listed, use only that chart and its restrictions, and meet the other inspection and operating requirements.
4. If it isn't listed, don't lift. Reinstall the counterweight according to the manufacturer's procedure and complete the required checks, or get direction from the manufacturer.

I can't tell from these regulations whether your crane can safely lift, swing, extend the boom or travel without counterweight. That includes moving it around the yard, since removing counterweight can affect more than lifting capacity. Check the manufacturer's instructions for those too.

response.text:
**Monthly running rope inspection, §1910.180(g)(1)**

- **Frequency and scope:** All ropes in use must get a thorough inspection at least once a month.
- **Who may perform it:** An **appointed or authorized person**.
- **What to evaluate:** Any deterioration causing appreciable loss of original strength must be carefully observed, and a determination made whether further use would be a safety hazard. Conditions that could cause such a loss include:
  - Reduced diameter below nominal from loss of core support, internal or external corrosion, or wear of outside wires
  - The number of broken outside wires, and how they are distributed or concentrated
  - Worn outside wires
  - Corroded or broken wires at end connections
  - Corroded, cracked, bent, worn or improperly applied end connections
  - Severe kinking, crushing, cutting or unstranding

**Documentation, §1910.180(g)(1)**

Prepare a certification record and keep it on file where readily available. It must include:
1. The date of inspection
2. The signature of the person who performed it
3. An identifier for the ropes inspected

**Related requirements, §1910.180(g)(2)**
- **Limited-travel areas:** Take particular care where rope may see heavy wear or broken wires, such as sections in contact with equalizer sheaves, other sheaves with limited rope travel, or saddles.
- **Idle rope:** If a crane's shutdown or storage has left its installed rope idle for **a month or more**, the rope needs a thorough inspection for all types of deterioration **before use**. An appointed or authorized person must perform it, and that person's approval is required for further use. A certification record is also required, with the date, the inspector's signature and a rope identifier.
- **Nonrotating rope:** Take particular care when inspecting it.

This answer covers general industry. For construction work, check the wire rope inspection rules in §1926.1413.

response.text:
**General industry (29 CFR 1910):** under **§1910.184(f)(5)(i)**, remove a wire rope sling from service **immediately** if it has either:
- **10 randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay**, or
- **5 broken wires in one strand in one rope lay**

Reaching either number fails the sling. Count how many breaks are in the worst lay, and how many of those are in the same strand. A rope lay is the length along the rope in which one strand makes a full wrap around it.

**Being under those counts doesn't mean it passes.** §1910.184(f)(5)(ii)–(vii) also requires removal for:
- Wear or scraping of one-third the original diameter of outside individual wires
- Kinking, crushing, birdcaging or other damage that distorts the rope structure
- Evidence of heat damage
- Cracked, deformed or worn end attachments
- Hooks opened more than 15% of the normal throat opening, measured at the narrowest point, or twisted more than 10° from the plane of the unbent hook
- Corrosion of the rope or end attachments

**Inspection:** §1910.184(d) requires a competent person to inspect the sling and its fastenings and attachments each day before use, with more inspections during use where service conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings must be removed immediately.

**On a construction job:** don't rely on the 10/5 rule above. Construction sling rules are in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart H (§1926.251), which is outside the regulations I answer from, so I can't give you its removal criteria. Check that section or ask your qualified rigger or safety lead. The wire rope criteria in Subpart CC, §1926.1413, are for crane ropes, so don't apply them to your choker.

Until you've confirmed which rule applies and checked the sling against it, tag it out and keep it out of use.

**Boom, upper and hook** (general industry mobile crane rule, §1910.180, transit precautions; check the exact paragraph in the current text):
- **Boom:** Carry it in line with the direction of travel.
- **Upper (superstructure):** Secure it against rotation. The exception is when negotiating turns with an operator in the cab, or when the boom is supported on a dolly.
- **Empty hook:** Lash or otherwise restrain it so it can't swing freely.

**Construction:** I don't know of a matching boom, upper and hook transit rule in Subpart CC, so don't treat the list above as a Subpart CC citation. You must follow the manufacturer's procedures applicable to the crane's operation (§1926.1417(a)). Check the manual for travel configuration, such as swing lock or pin, boom position, outriggers, counterweight, tires and travel speed. I don't have your crane's procedures.

**Power lines, traveling with no load on a construction site (§1926.1411):**
- **Lowered boom:** §1926.1411 covers travel with the boom/mast and boom/mast support system lowered enough to maintain these Table T clearances (§1926.1411(b)(1)):

| Line voltage | Minimum clearance |
|---|---|
| Up to 0.75 kV | 4 ft |
| Over 0.75 to 50 kV | 6 ft |
| Over 50 to 345 kV | 10 ft |
| Over 345 to 750 kV | 16 ft |
| Over 750 to 1,000 kV | 20 ft |
| Over 1,000 kV | Set by the utility owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer |

- **Boom not lowered that far:** §1926.1408 applies instead (§1926.1411(a)).
- **Movement:** Account for how speed and terrain affect boom and equipment movement (§1926.1411(b)(2)).
- **Spotter:** If any part of the equipment will get closer than 20 ft to a line while traveling, use a dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the operator and meets the other conditions in §1926.1411(b)(3).
- **Poor visibility or night:** Illuminate the lines or use another way to identify their location, in addition to the other measures (§1926.1411(b)(4)).

**Public roads:** These OSHA regulations don't tell me the DOT or state requirements, such as permits, height and weight limits, escorts or road securement.

If you mean traveling **with a load**, that has separate requirements (§1926.1417(u)).

These answers are from the general industry sling rule, §1910.184, for **alloy steel chain slings**.

**How often: thorough periodic inspection**
- Do it on a regular schedule, **at least once every 12 months** (§1910.184(e)(3)(i)). Twelve months is the maximum interval.
- Set a shorter interval if warranted, based on (§1910.184(e)(3)(i)):
  - how often the sling is used
  - how severe the service conditions are
  - the nature of the lifts
  - experience with the service life of slings used in similar circumstances
- A competent person designated by the employer must check for wear, defective welds, deformation and increase in length. A sling with such defects or deterioration must be **removed from service immediately** (§1910.184(e)(3)(iii)).
- This is in addition to the daily before-use inspection, and any inspections during use that service conditions call for (§1910.184(d)).

**Records**
- **Inspection:** Make and keep a record of the **most recent month** each sling was thoroughly inspected, and have it available for examination (§1910.184(e)(3)(ii)).
- **Proof test:** New, repaired or reconditioned slings, including all welded components, must be proof tested before use by the sling manufacturer or an equivalent entity. You must **keep the proof test certificate** and have it available for examination (§1910.184(e)(4)).

**If this is construction work:** §1910.184 is the general industry rule. Construction rigging requirements for slings are in §1926.251, which is outside the regulations I answer from. Subpart CC also refers to it for rigging (see §1926.1404(r) for assembly/disassembly), so don't assume the intervals or records above are all that apply to a construction job. Check §1926.251 directly.

**If it was heated above 1000°F, no. It must be permanently removed from service, even if it looks fine** (§1910.184(e)(6)). The rule sets no exception for passing a visual inspection, and it applies to alloy steel chain slings.

**Since you don't know how hot it got:** take it out of service now and tag it so nobody uses it. As a precaution, don't return it to use unless you can reliably establish that it never went above 1000°F. If you can't, I recommend retiring it. That's my safety advice; the paragraph itself doesn't say how to handle an unknown temperature. These regulations also give me no way to determine the peak temperature from its appearance, and a proof test shouldn't be used to clear a sling that may have been overheated.

- **Over 600°F:** for exposure to service temperatures above 600°F, working load limits must be reduced according to the chain or sling manufacturer's recommendations (§1910.184(e)(6)). I can't determine that from these regulations.
- **Inspection:** a competent person must inspect the sling, fastenings and attachments for damage or defects each day before use, with additional inspections during use where service conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings must be removed from service immediately (§1910.184(d)).

**Fiber core sling: permanently remove it from service.** Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades must be permanently removed if exposed to temperatures **above 200°F** (§1910.184(f)(3)(i)). At about 250°F, it can't go back into use, even if it looks undamaged or has cooled. The estimate is well above the limit. Take it out now so no one else uses it.

**IWRC sling: the rule is different.** For nonfiber core wire rope slings of any grade, used **above 400°F or below −60°F**, you must follow the sling manufacturer's recommendations for use at that temperature (§1910.184(f)(3)(ii)). IWRC is a nonfiber core, so 250°F alone triggers neither that requirement nor removal. The 400°F figure isn't an automatic discard limit.

An IWRC sling still has to meet these conditions:
- **Inspection:** A competent person designated by the employer must inspect the sling and its fastenings and attachments each day before use, with additional inspections during use where service conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings must be immediately removed from service (§1910.184(d)).
- **Heat damage:** Evidence of heat damage requires immediate removal, whatever temperature you estimated (§1910.184(f)(5)(iv)). The other criteria in §1910.184(f)(5) also apply.
- **Other components:** These temperature figures don't tell you the limits for any other coating, fitting or component. Check the manufacturer's information, since I can't determine those limits from these regulations.

**Scope:** These citations are from the general industry sling standard. If this was construction work, sling requirements fall under a construction rule outside the regulations I answer from (see also §1926.1425 and Subpart CC's other rigging provisions for crane work). I therefore can't confirm the construction sling temperature rule here.

- **Nylon: No.** Nylon web slings must not be used where **fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids of acids or phenolics** are present (§1910.184(i)(6)(i)). Your acid mist is covered.
- **Polyester: The acid mist alone doesn't rule it out under this rule.** Polyester and polypropylene web slings are prohibited where **fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids of caustics** are present (§1910.184(i)(6)(ii)). Check for caustics in the area, such as from nearby cleaning or neutralizing operations.
- **Aluminum fittings: It matters if caustics are present.** Web slings with aluminum fittings must not be used where caustic fumes, vapors, sprays, mists or liquids are present (§1910.184(i)(6)(iii)). That paragraph doesn't prohibit them for acids, but this **doesn't show they're compatible with your acid**. Confirm that with the sling manufacturer, giving the acid, its concentration and the temperature. Do the same for the polyester webbing and stitching.

- **Temperature:** Polyester and nylon web slings must not be used above **180°F**, and polypropylene above **200°F** (§1910.184(i)(7)).

- **Removal from service:** Immediately remove a synthetic web sling with **acid or caustic burns**; melting or charring; snags, punctures, tears or cuts; broken or worn stitches; or distorted fittings (§1910.184(i)(9)).

**No. Repaired or reconditioned fiber rope slings are prohibited.** Only fiber rope slings made from new rope may be used (§1910.184(h)(5)). This section covers both natural and synthetic fiber rope slings.

**Remove a sling from service immediately if it has any of these (§1910.184(h)(4)):**
- Abnormal wear
- Powdered fiber between strands
- Broken or cut fibers
- Variations in the size or roundness of strands
- Discoloration or rotting
- Distortion of hardware in the sling

This rule is from the 1910 general industry standard. Construction sling rules are in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart H, which is outside the regulations I answer from, so I can't say from these what applies to a construction job.

Synthetic **web** slings have separate repair rules (§1910.184(i)), so don't apply the fiber rope ban to them.

**Under §1910.184(i)(8), a repaired synthetic web sling must meet these requirements:**

- **Who repairs it:** It can't be used unless a **sling manufacturer or an equivalent entity** repaired it (§1910.184(i)(8)(i)).
- **Proof test:** Before it returns to service, the manufacturer or equivalent entity must proof test **each repaired sling to twice its rated capacity** (§1910.184(i)(8)(ii)).
- **Records:** The employer must **keep a certificate of the proof test and make it available for examination** (§1910.184(i)(8)(ii)).
- **No temporary repairs:** Slings, **including webbing and fittings**, that have been repaired temporarily **may not be used** (§1910.184(i)(8)(iii)).

Once back in service, the sling and its fastenings and attachments need a competent person's inspection for damage or defects **each day before use**, with additional inspections during use where service conditions warrant (§1910.184(d)).

These are the Part 1910 (general industry) rules. For construction, sling requirements fall outside Subpart CC's own text and the other sections I cover, so I can't state the construction sling repair rules here.

**No, the counts differ.** Poly rope is synthetic, so it needs more tucks than manila (§1910.184(h)(3)(i)-(ii)).

| Rope | Eye splice, minimum | Short splice, minimum |
|---|---|---|
| Synthetic (including poly) | **4 full tucks** | 8 full tucks (4 each side of center line) |
| Manila | **3 full tucks** | 6 full tucks (3 each side of center line) |

Other requirements under §1910.184(h)(3):
- **Manufacturer:** Also follow any additional manufacturer recommendations.
- **Tails:** Don't trim them flush with the rope next to the full tucks.
  - For rope **under 1 in.** diameter, tails must project at least **6 rope diameters** past the last full tuck.
  - For rope **1 in. and larger**, they must project at least **6 in.**
  - If a projecting tail interferes with use, taper it and splice it into the rope body with at least **2 additional tucks**. This takes about 6 rope diameters of tail.
- **Length:** Clear rope between eye splices must be at least **10 rope diameters**.
- **Eye size:** The included angle at the splice can't exceed **60°** when the eye is over the load or support.
- **Substitutes:** Don't use knots instead of splices, or clamps not designed specifically for fiber rope.

These citations are from the general industry sling standard. Construction sling rules are in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart H, which is outside the regulations I answer from. If this is a construction job, check that text.

**General industry (29 CFR 1910.184):** a **competent person designated by the employer** checks slings.

- **When:** **each day before use**, covering the sling and all fastenings and attachments for damage or defects (§1910.184(d)). The wording is daily, not every shift.
- **During use:** additional inspections are required where service conditions warrant (§1910.184(d)).
- **Damaged or defective slings:** remove them from service immediately (§1910.184(d)).

**Alloy steel chain slings** also need a **thorough periodic inspection** (§1910.184(e)(3)):
- **How often:** set it based on how often the sling is used, severity of service conditions, the nature of the lifts, and experience with the service life of slings used in similar circumstances. The interval can **never be more than 12 months**.
- **Records:** the employer must make and keep a record of the most recent month each sling was thoroughly inspected, and have it available for examination.

**Construction:** I can't give you the sling inspection frequency for construction from the regulations I cover. General construction rigging rules are in 29 CFR 1926 Subpart H (see §1926.251), so check that text. Don't assume the 1910.184 daily rule is the construction rule.

**No. Under OSHA's construction crane rule, an engineer's sign-off isn't automatically required** when more than one crane or derrick supports the load.

**Construction (§1926.1432):**
- **Plan:** The lift must be planned before it begins (§1926.1432(a)). A **qualified person** must develop the plan (§1926.1432(a)(1)).
- **Content:** The plan must be designed to ensure that Subpart CC's requirements are met (§1926.1432(a)(2)).
- **Engineering:** If the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure it's provided (§1926.1432(a)(3)).
- **Lift director:** The lift must be directed by someone who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person assisted by one or more qualified persons (§1926.1432(b)(1)).
- **Meeting:** The lift director must review the plan in a meeting with all workers involved in the operation (§1926.1432(b)(2)).

A "qualified person" doesn't have to be a licensed engineer. The definition covers someone who, by a recognized degree, certificate or professional standing, **or** by extensive knowledge, training and experience, has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve problems relating to the subject matter, work or project (§1926.1401).

**General industry, for crawler, locomotive and truck cranes (§1910.180(h)(3)(iv)):** When two or more cranes lift one load, one designated person must be responsible for the operation. That person must analyze it and instruct everyone involved in positioning, rigging the load and the movements to be made. This paragraph doesn't require an engineer's sign-off.

These regulations don't settle whether state rules, contracts, site or company policy, or manufacturer procedures require an engineer for your lift.

**No. In construction, the office trailer isn't enough.** Under §1926.1417(c)(1), the procedures that apply to operating the equipment must be **readily available in the cab at all times for use by the operator**. This includes:
- Rated capacities (load charts)
- Recommended operating speeds
- Special hazard warnings
- Instructions
- The operator's manual

You can keep extra copies in the trailer, but they don't replace what has to be in the cab.

**Electronic load charts:** If rated capacities are available in the cab only electronically and a failure makes them inaccessible, the operator must immediately cease operations or follow safe shut-down procedures until they're available again, electronically or in another form (§1926.1417(c)(2)).

**General industry (crawler, locomotive and truck cranes):** §1910.180(c)(2) requires a durable, clearly legible rating chart with each crane, **securely fixed to the crane cab** where the operator can easily see it while seated at the control station.

**Yes, in construction under Subpart CC, if you have a suitable device. The cutoff is 75%** (§1926.1417(o)(3)(ii)).

- **Devices allowed:** a load weighing device, load moment indicator (LMI), rated capacity indicator or rated capacity limiter.
- **Which 75%:** it's 75% of the maximum rated capacity **at the longest radius you'll use during the lift**, not at the pick radius. Check the whole path, including the set point, using the load chart for your configuration. For example, if the chart allows 20,000 lb at that longest radius, your threshold is 15,000 lb.
- **If it exceeds 75%:** don't proceed with the lift until you verify the weight under §1926.1417(o)(3)(i). That means a reliable source (such as the load's manufacturer), a reliable calculation (such as measured steel dimensions and known per-foot weight) or other equally reliable means. If you ask for this information, it must be provided before the lift.

**Watch for**
- An LMI percentage at the pick radius may not be the percentage you need. Compare the load with 75% of the capacity at the longest radius, and account for how your device and chart treat deductions such as the hook block and rigging.
- The crane's rated capacity still can't be exceeded (§1926.1417(o)(1)).
- This check only addresses crane capacity. It doesn't show that your slings and rigging are adequate for an unknown weight. Under general industry rules, slings can't be loaded beyond rated capacity (§1910.184(c)(4)).
- If you have a safety concern, you have authority to stop and refuse to handle the load until a qualified person determines that safety is assured (§1926.1418).

**General industry:** this 75% method comes from the construction rule. Don't assume it applies to work under §1910.179 or §1910.180, which have their own rated load limits.

For how to read your particular LMI, or what to do if it isn't working properly, you'll need the manufacturer's information. I can't answer the device-specific operation from these regulations.

**What OSHA does require** (assuming construction work under Subpart CC):

- **Manufacturer criteria:** Equipment that has had a repair or adjustment relating to safe operation must be inspected by a qualified person after the work and before initial use (§1926.1412(b)(1)). The rotation mechanism is one of the listed examples. The qualified person must determine that the repair or adjustment meets manufacturer equipment criteria where they are applicable and available (§1926.1412(b)(1)(i)(A)).
- **If manufacturer criteria are unavailable or inapplicable:** The qualified person must determine whether a registered professional engineer (RPE) is needed to develop criteria. If not, the employer must ensure the qualified person develops them. If so, the employer must ensure an RPE develops them (§1926.1412(b)(1)(i)(B)).
- **Inspection and testing:** The inspection must include functional testing of the repaired or adjusted components and other components that may be affected (§1926.1412(b)(1)(ii)). The crane must not be used until the inspection shows the repair or adjustment meets the applicable criteria (§1926.1412(b)(1)(iii)).

If the crane is used in general industry, §1910.180 applies instead, and the paragraphs above aren't the governing citations.

**Don't set up yet.** The equipment must not be assembled or used unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough that, with supporting materials if needed, the **manufacturer's specifications for support and levelness** are met (§1926.1402(b)). The drainage requirement doesn't apply to marshes or wetlands. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies (in marshes or wetlands) and similar devices (§1926.1402(a)(2)).

**What happens next**
- If you (or the A/D director) determine the ground doesn't meet (b), **your employer must discuss the needed ground preparations with the controlling entity**. The goal is to meet (b), using suitable supporting materials if necessary (§1926.1402(e)). Tell your employer so that can happen.
- Whenever there's a safety concern, you must have **authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured** (§1926.1418).

**Who fixes the ground**
- The **controlling entity** must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided (§1926.1402(c)(1)). This is the prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager or other legal entity with overall responsibility for the project's construction, including planning, quality and completion (§1926.1401).
- It must also tell the equipment user and operator where hazards are beneath the setup area, such as voids, tanks or utilities. This applies if the hazards are identified in documents it possesses, on or off site (such as drawings or soil analyses), or are otherwise known to it (§1926.1402(c)(2)).

**If there's no controlling entity**
- The **employer with authority at the site to make or arrange for the ground preparations** must meet the (c)(1) duty to ensure they're provided (§1926.1402(d)). That isn't automatically the crane company or your employer.
- Paragraph (d) transfers **only (c)(1)**. It doesn't reassign the (c)(2) duty to disclose underground hazards.
- Paragraph (e) names only the controlling entity for the discussion, and doesn't say who it's held with if there isn't one. As a practical step, not a stated requirement of (e), your employer should raise it with the employer identified under (d).
- The ground **still must meet (b)** before assembly or use.

**Limits:** These regulations don't give the required bearing capacity or mat size for your crane. That takes the manufacturer's specifications and information about your site. §1926.1402 also excludes railroad cranes used on FRA-regulated track in the general railroad system, if they comply with applicable FRA requirements (§1926.1402(f)). This answer is for construction work under Subpart CC.

I can't tell you what that LICCON code means or how to clear it from these regulations. Error codes and fault-clearing steps are manufacturer information, and Subpart CC doesn't define them. Check the LICCON diagnostics and operator's manual for your serial number, or call Liebherr service. Give them the exact code as displayed, the crane's serial number, the configuration and boom state, and what you were doing when it appeared.

These OSHA rules apply in the meantime if you're doing construction work:

- **Check whether it must come out of service.** If an inspection finds a safety device not working properly, it must be taken out of service and operations must not begin until it works (§1926.1415(a)). If the device fails during operations, the operator must safely stop (§1926.1415(a)). This applies to the listed safety devices. Operational aids follow §1926.1416.

If this is general industry work, the mobile crane rule is §1910.180, which also won't decode the fault.

If you learn from Liebherr or the manual which sensor or device the code points to, tell me and I can go through the §1926.1416 or §1926.1415 requirements for it.

**I can't give you the Manitowoc 2250 pin-pulling order or blocking setup from these regulations.** Subpart CC doesn't contain model-specific procedures. Get the 2250 operator and assembly/disassembly manual for your serial number and boom configuration, or contact Manitowoc or its dealer. Don't rely on a generic sequence or one from another crane.

**What OSHA requires**
- **Procedures:** You must follow either the manufacturer's procedures or employer procedures (§1926.1403). Employer procedures must meet §1926.1406.
- **Supervision:** An assembly/disassembly (A/D) director who meets the competent and qualified person criteria, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons, must direct the work (§1926.1404(a)). The director must understand the applicable procedures (§1926.1404(b)) and review them immediately before starting, unless the director understands them and has applied them to the same equipment type and configuration (§1926.1404(c)).
- **Crew briefing:** Before starting, crew members must understand their tasks, the hazards, and the hazardous positions or locations to avoid (§1926.1404(d)(1)).
- **Under the boom:** Employees must not be under the boom, jib or other components while pins or similar devices are being removed (§1926.1404(f)(1)). The exception applies only where the employer demonstrates that site constraints require it. The A/D director must then use procedures that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure (§1926.1404(f)(2)).
- **Blocking material:** Its size, amount, condition and stacking method must be sufficient to sustain the loads and maintain stability (§1926.1404(h)(2)).
- **Blocking location:** When supporting lattice booms or components, blocking must be placed to protect their structural integrity and prevent dangerous movement and collapse (§1926.1404(h)(3)).
- **Pin removal:** Boom sections, boom suspension systems and components must be rigged or supported to maintain stability when pins are removed (§1926.1404(h)(7)).

These requirements don't tell you which 2250 pins to pull first or where to put the blocking. If the applicable procedure isn't available to the A/D director, resolve that before pulling any pins.

  - It must include functional testing of the repaired or adjusted parts and other components that may be affected (§1926.1412(b)(2)).
  - The equipment must not be used until the inspection shows it meets those criteria (§1926.1412(b)(3)).

If the crane is in general industry service, tell me how it's configured and used. That affects whether §1910.180 or another rule applies.

  - Put all controllers in the off position.
  - Open the main or emergency switch and lock it in the open position.
  - Place warning or "out of order" signs on the crane, and on the floor beneath or on the hook where visible from the floor.

I can't tell you whether it will make the pick. That depends on your Elliott's load chart for its exact model and configuration, which I don't have, and the 40-ton rating doesn't tell you the capacity at 50 ft.

**What OSHA requires before the lift** (Subpart CC, construction):
- **Capacity:** Don't exceed rated capacity (§1926.1417(o)(1)).
- **Load weight:** Verify it from a recognized industry source (such as the manufacturer) or a recognized calculation method, or with a load-weighing device or similar means. With a weighing device, if the load exceeds 75% of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius you'll use, don't lift it more than a few inches until you've confirmed from the rating chart that it's within capacity (§1926.1417(o)(3)). Treat 6,500 lb as unconfirmed until you've done this.
- **Charts and procedures:** They must be readily available in the cab (§1926.1417(c)).
- **Ground:** It must be firm, drained and graded enough, with supporting materials if needed, to meet the manufacturer's support and level specs (§1926.1402(b)).
- **Outriggers** (§1926.1404(q)):
  - Extend or deploy them as the load chart requires.
  - Set them to remove the weight from the wheels, except for locomotive cranes.
  - Attach floats, if used, to the outriggers.
  - Blocking under them must be able to support the loads, stay stable and sit under the float or pad (or the outer bearing surface of the extended beam).
- **Power lines:** Before setup, identify the work zone and determine whether any part of the equipment, load line or load could get within 20 ft of a line. If so, follow the §1926.1408(a)(2) options. Lines over 350 kV have further rules (§1926.1409).

**To check the chart** (practical steps; the manufacturer's chart notes control):
1. Use the chart matching your outrigger setup and any counterweight.
2. Measure radius the way the chart defines it, usually from the center of rotation. Check the farthest radius in the whole swing, both pick and set. "50 ft out" from the truck or building may not be 50 ft radius.
3. Check boom length, boom angle, jib status and working area (over side, rear or front).
4. Add whatever the chart notes say to deduct, such as the hook block, rigging, spreader bar and stowed or erected jib, to the unit's weight.
5. If you're between listed values, follow the chart's instructions. Don't assume you can interpolate.

If this isn't construction work, such as a like-for-like maintenance replacement, 29 CFR 1910.180 may apply instead. It also bars loading beyond the rated load (§1910.180(h)(3)(i)).

If you send the chart page and its notes, along with your boom length, radius, configuration and rigging weights, I can help you total the load and compare it to the listed value. The operator still has to verify it against the actual chart in the truck.

**The closest OSHA text is §1910.184(i)(9), "Removal from service," for synthetic web slings.** It is a general industry rule written for web slings, not roundslings, and it isn't B30.9's list. It requires immediate removal if any of these are present:

- **(i)** Acid or caustic burns
- **(ii)** Melting or charring of any part of the sling surface
- **(iii)** Snags, punctures, tears or cuts
- **(iv)** Broken or worn stitches
- **(v)** Distortion of fittings

§1910.184(d) also requires a competent person to inspect each sling and its fastenings and attachments each day before use, with additional inspections during use where service conditions warrant. Damaged or defective slings must be removed from service immediately.

For construction work, rigging requirements fall under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart H (§1926.251), which is outside the regulations I cover. §1926.1404(r) in Subpart CC addresses synthetic slings during assembly and disassembly, but it isn't a roundsling removal list.

For the B30.9 criteria, check the roundsling chapter in a current copy of ASME B30.9. Also follow the sling manufacturer's inspection and removal instructions.

**I can't give you that capacity from these regulations.** OSHA doesn't publish capacities or a general derating percentage for a Link-Belt 238 HSL at 2° list, 160 ft of boom and 70 ft radius. Don't use the land chart, or a rule-of-thumb percentage taken off it, for barge work.

**What applies in construction (§1926.1437, floating cranes and land cranes on barges; the land-crane provisions are in paragraph (n), but check subparagraph wording against the current text):**
- **Reduced rating:** The land-based rated capacity must be modified to account for the added loading from list, trim, wave action and wind.
- **Who does it:** The crane manufacturer or a qualified person must make the modification. If a qualified person does it, that person needs expertise with land cranes on flotation.
- **Conditions evaluated:** The rating has to fit this crane on this flotation platform under the expected environmental conditions. List and trim must stay within the limits on which that rating depends.
- **Related requirements:** The section also addresses load charts, list and trim indication, and securing or physically restraining the land crane on the barge. Review the whole section before setup.

**What to give the manufacturer or qualified person:**
- **Crane:** serial number, configuration, boom and any jib, counterweight, crawler position, reeving and the land load chart.
- **Barge:** a 120 × 40 ft deck size isn't enough. They'll likely need hull depth, lightship weight and center of gravity, freeboard and draft, structural and deck strength data, and tank or ballast conditions, including free surface.
- **Setup:** crane location and orientation, matting, securing arrangement and other deck loads.
- **Lift and site:** loads, radii, swing arcs, wind, waves and current.

Ask for a **barge-specific load chart** that states its list and trim limits, permitted radii and swing positions, crane location, and environmental limits. Check both list and trim, including their change as the loaded boom swings. A 2° list figure alone doesn't establish a capacity.

If this work isn't construction, such as maritime cargo handling, different rules may apply.

I can't answer whether you can sue the GC or the crane company. That's a legal question about liability and property damage, usually governed by state law and possibly by contracts or insurance, and the OSHA crane regulations I work from don't address it. A local attorney or your auto insurer can advise you. If you were parked there for work, your employer may also need to know.

These steps can help preserve your claim:
- Photograph the damage, the load, the barricade and where your truck was parked.
- Write down the date, time, witnesses, and the names of the companies involved.
- Report it in writing to the GC and the crane company, and keep copies.
- Get a repair estimate.
- Check any deadlines with your insurer or attorney.

On the OSHA side, Subpart CC has rules that may relate to the incident, though I wouldn't treat any of them as deciding who pays:
- **Qualified rigger:** §1926.1425(c) requires rigging by a qualified rigger when employees are in the fall zone and engaged in hooking, unhooking or guiding a load, or doing the initial connection of a load to a component or structure. §1926.1404(r)(1) also requires a qualified rigger when rigging is used for assembly or disassembly.
- **Keeping people clear:** §1926.1425 also limits who may be in the fall zone. It protects employees, not parked vehicles.

Being outside the barricade doesn't by itself establish fault under these rules. If you tell me what happened during the lift, such as how the load was being set down, whether anyone was near it or whether this was assembly work, I can tell you which crane requirements may apply.

**I can't tell you the fine from these regulations.** Subpart CC and §§1910.179, .180 and .184 don't set penalty amounts. Check the **citation and penalty notice** for the proposed amount, the classification of each violation, the standard cited and your response deadline. **The deadline to contest is short, so check it now.** For questions about contesting or reducing the penalty, talk to the OSHA Area Office or an attorney. If a State Plan agency issued the citation, follow its instructions.

**If this was construction work, §1926.1412(e) requires:**
- **Frequency:** an inspection each month the equipment is in service, covering the shift inspection items in §1926.1412(d) (§1926.1412(e)(1)).
- **Records:** the employer that conducts the inspection must document and keep (§1926.1412(e)(3)(i)):
  - the items checked and the results
  - the inspector's name and signature
  - the date
- **Retention:** at least **3 months** (§1926.1412(e)(3)(ii)).

Wire rope has additional monthly inspection provisions in §1926.1413(b).

**If this was general industry work,** the monthly requirements differ by crane type and component. For example, see §1910.179(j) and (m) for overhead and gantry cranes, and §1910.180(d) and (g) for crawler, locomotive and truck cranes.

Compare the cited paragraph with what actually happened, including when the crane was in service and whether any records exist for those months. Don't create or backdate records for missed inspections.

**I can't clear you to operate from these regulations, and while the medication is making you dizzy, I advise staying out of the seat until a medical professional clears you.**

**What the regulations cover:** I know of no provision in Subpart CC or §§1910.179–.180 that lists blood pressure drugs or says whether you're medically fit while taking one. That **doesn't mean you're allowed to run.** §1926.1427 covers operator training, certification and evaluation, but passing those doesn't answer this question. Your employer's policy, certification or site medical requirements, other standards, or DOT rules if they apply to you may add requirements that I can't address here.

**If a safety concern comes up:** Under §1926.1418, whenever there's a safety concern, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured. If you're in the middle of a lift and feel dizzy, stop as soon as you safely can. Don't leave a load unsecured or the crane improperly unattended (§1926.1417(e)). A qualified person's determination under §1926.1418 isn't a substitute for medical clearance.

**What to do before your next shift:**
- **Call your doctor or pharmacist today.** Tell them you run a crawler crane, you've been dizzy, and what else you take, including over-the-counter drugs. Ask whether you can safely operate and climb on and off the machine, and what needs to happen before you return.
- **Don't stop or change the dose on your own** without talking to them.
- **Tell your supervisor** you may not be fit to operate, and check the company's fitness-for-duty policy. Ask about other work, but avoid driving, climbing or other hazardous tasks while dizzy.
- **Don't drive yourself** anywhere while you're dizzy.

**Get emergency care (call 911)** if you faint or have chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, confusion, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, vision changes, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat. This is general safety advice, not from the crane regulations.

**I can't answer whether workers' comp will pay or can deny your claim.** The OSHA crane regulations I work from don't cover comp eligibility. That falls under your state's workers' compensation law (or a federal program, for some workers), and I don't want to guess about your claim.

**Steps to take now:**
- **Report the injury to your employer promptly, in writing,** and keep a copy. Comp claims have notice and filing deadlines that vary, so don't wait to see if your back improves.

Whether you could be jailed is a question of criminal law and legal liability, and I can't answer it from the OSHA crane regulations. A criminal defense attorney can, and the answer may depend on your state and the facts.

What the construction rules do say about people under the load (29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC):

- **Routing, §1926.1425(a):** Where available, hoisting routes that minimize employees' exposure to hoisted loads must be used, to the extent consistent with public safety.
- **Fall zone, §1926.1425(b):** While the operator isn't moving a suspended load, no employee may be in the fall zone. The exceptions are employees hooking, unhooking or guiding the load, doing the initial attachment of the load to a component or structure, or operating a concrete hopper or bucket.
- **Hooking, unhooking, guiding and initial connection, §1926.1425(c):** When these employees are in the fall zone, the load must be rigged to prevent unintentional displacement. Hooks with self-closing latches or the equivalent must be used, except for "J" hooks used for setting wooden trusses. A qualified rigger must rig the materials.
- **Receiving a load, §1926.1425(d):** Only employees needed to receive it may be in the fall zone while it's being landed.
- **Other cases:** §1926.1425(e) has conditions for tilt-up and tilt-down operations, and steel erection is also affected by §1926.753(d), which is outside Subpart CC.
- **Stop authority, §1926.1418:** Whenever there is a safety concern, you have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety is assured.

These rules cover construction work. They don't settle what penalty or criminal charge a particular person could face. If someone has already been hurt or killed, talk to an attorney about your own situation.

Don't assume a later threat or firing will be needed before the time starts. Call 1-800-321-OSHA (6742) or go to whistleblowers.gov, and ask whether the threat itself counts and what your deadline is. State-plan rules or other laws may also apply, so ask about those or talk to an employment lawyer.

**What the crane rules say (construction, Subpart CC):**
- **Authority to refuse, §1926.1418:** "Whenever there is a concern as to safety, the operator must have the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until a qualified person has determined that safety has been assured." This applies to you as the operator. It doesn't itself set out a retaliation complaint process or remedy.
- **Ground conditions, §1926.1402(b):** The equipment must not be assembled or used unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough that, with supporting materials if necessary, the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level are met.
- **Who provides it, §1926.1402(c):** The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are made. It must also inform the crane user and operator of known underground hazards, as that paragraph specifies.
- **If the ground is inadequate, §1926.1402(e):** If the A/D (assembly/disassembly) director or the operator determines that ground conditions don't meet §1926.1402(b), that person's employer must discuss it with the controlling entity so that the requirements can be met with suitable supporting materials or other means.

If this was general industry work under §1910.180 instead, don't rely on the construction citations above.

- Any later discipline, lost hours or schedule changes

Keep any related texts or photos that you're allowed to have. If you're asked to make the pick again and the concern isn't resolved, raise it clearly as a safety concern, cite §1926.1418 if it's construction work, and ask for a qualified person's determination.

**Crane operators in construction (Subpart CC)** have separate requirements for certification and employer evaluation:

- **Certification:** Certification from an accredited testing organization (§1926.1427(d)) or an audited employer program (§1926.1427(e)) is valid for **5 years**. Audited employer program certification isn't portable to another employer.

**Ground conditions, §1926.1402**
- **Support:** The crane must not be assembled or used unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough that, with supporting materials if necessary, the manufacturer's specifications for **adequate support and degree of level** are met (§1926.1402(b)). This is a medical emergency, and a crush injury can be worse than it looks. These are general first aid basics, not from the crane regulations.

**Right now**
- **Call 911** if you haven't already. Say it's a crush injury, and say if he's still pinned and for how long. Send someone to meet EMS.
- **Stop the crane and keep it from swinging or moving.** Make sure the area is safe before anyone goes in.
- **If he's still pinned,** tell the dispatcher and follow their instructions. Releasing a long or severe crush can cause sudden, dangerous effects. Don't swing the crane to free him without thinking it through, because that can injure him further. If he's in immediate danger or bleeding badly where you can reach it, act on that and tell the dispatcher.
- **Control severe bleeding** with firm, direct pressure. If an arm bleed is life-threatening and pressure won't stop it, or he has an amputation, put a **tourniquet** 2–3 inches above the wound, not on a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, note the time, and don't loosen it.
- **Check breathing and responsiveness.** If he's unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED.

**While waiting**
- Keep him still and don't straighten the arm. Support it in the position you found it. If you suspect a head, neck or back injury, don't move him unless he's in danger.
- Remove rings and watches before swelling sets in, if it's easy to do. Don't pull off anything stuck or embedded.
- Cover open wounds with a clean dressing.
- Treat for shock: keep him lying down if his injuries allow, and keep him warm.
- Give nothing to eat or drink. Don't massage the arm.
- Watch him closely, and tell EMS about numbness, color changes, increasing pain or swelling, and how long he was pinned. **He needs medical evaluation even if he says he's fine.**

Follow the dispatcher and anyone on site trained in first aid.

**Afterward (regulations):** §1926.1424(a)(2) requires swing radius hazard areas to be marked and barricaded to keep employees from being struck or pinched/crushed. There are limited alternatives in (a)(2)(ii) when barricading isn't feasible. Check that setup before work resumes. Preserve the details of the scene, and have your employer check OSHA's injury reporting deadlines, which are in Part 1904, outside the regulations I cover.
